prompt: **Problem 1.1.1.** Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ with $\dim V=n<\infty$, where $\dim V$ is the smallest size of a spanning set (a basis is a spanning set of size $\dim V$). Show that any linearly independent set of $n$ vectors in $V$ is a basis of $V$.
answer: Independent $n$ vectors that did not span could be extended to $n+1$ independent vectors, impossible in a space spanned by $n$ vectors.

solutions.title: Counting unknowns and equations
solutions.body:
**Lemma.** If $V$ is spanned by $w_1,\dots,w_n$, then any $n+1$ vectors $u_0,\dots,u_n\in V$ are linearly dependent.

Write $u_j=\sum_{i=1}^n a_{ij}w_i$. The system $\sum_{j=0}^{n} c_j a_{ij}=0$ ($i=1,\dots,n$) has $n$ equations and $n+1$ unknowns $c_j$, so it has a nonzero solution. Then $\sum_j c_ju_j=\sum_i\big(\sum_j c_ja_{ij}\big)w_i=0$ is a nontrivial relation.

**Proof of the claim.** Let $v_1,\dots,v_n$ be independent and suppose they do not span $V$. Pick $v\in V\setminus\operatorname{span}\{v_1,\dots,v_n\}$. Then $v_1,\dots,v_n,v$ are independent: in a relation $\sum c_iv_i+cv=0$ we must have $c=0$ (otherwise $v$ lies in the span), and then all $c_i=0$. But $V$ is spanned by $n=\dim V$ vectors, so the lemma says any $n+1$ vectors are dependent, a contradiction. Hence $v_1,\dots,v_n$ span $V$ and, being independent, form a basis. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 1.1.2.** Show that $\mathbb R[x]$ is a real vector space and that $\mathbb C[x]$ is a complex vector space, where $F[x]$ is the set of polynomials of finite degree with coefficients in $F$ (with the usual addition and scalar multiplication). Is $\mathbb R[x]$ a complex vector space? Is $\mathbb C[x]$ a real vector space?
answer: $\mathbb R[x]$ is real and $\mathbb C[x]$ is complex; $\mathbb R[x]$ is not a complex vector space (not closed under multiplication by $i$); $\mathbb C[x]$ is a real vector space.

solutions.title: Check closure
solutions.body:
For a field $F$, the sum of two polynomials in $F[x]$ and the product of a polynomial by $c\in F$ are polynomials in $F[x]$ (coefficients stay in $F$ because $F$ is closed under $+$ and $\cdot$). The zero polynomial is the zero element, $-p$ gives inverses, and distributivity and associativity of scalar multiplication are inherited from the field axioms coefficientwise. So $\mathbb R[x]$ is a real and $\mathbb C[x]$ a complex vector space.

- $\mathbb R[x]$ **over $\mathbb C$**: no. $1\in\mathbb R[x]$ but $i\cdot1=i\notin\mathbb R[x]$, so it is not closed under complex scalars.
- $\mathbb C[x]$ **over $\mathbb R$**: yes. Real multiples of complex polynomials are complex polynomials, and all axioms hold because they hold for complex scalars, in particular for real ones. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 1.2.1(i).** Fix $N\in\mathbb N$ and let $F_N$ be the space of polynomials $a(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{N}a_nx^n$ over $F$ (degree at most $N$). Determine with proof whether the map $a(x)\mapsto a(x)+a(1)$ from $F_N$ to $F[x]$ is linear.
answer: Linear.

solutions.title: Check additivity and homogeneity
solutions.body:
Write $\alpha a+\beta b$ for the polynomial with coefficients $\alpha a_n+\beta b_n$. Evaluation at $1$ is linear: $(\alpha a+\beta b)(1)=\alpha a(1)+\beta b(1)$. Hence
$$f_1(\alpha a+\beta b)=\alpha a+\beta b+\big(\alpha a(1)+\beta b(1)\big)=\alpha f_1(a)+\beta f_1(b).$$
Also $f_1(\alpha a)=\alpha f_1(a)$ is the case $\beta=0$. So $f_1$ is linear. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 1.2.1(ii).** Fix $N\in\mathbb N$ and let $F_N$ be the space of polynomials $a(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{N}a_nx^n$ over $F$ (degree at most $N$). Determine with proof whether the map $a(x)\mapsto a(x)+a(1)x^{N+1}$ from $F_N$ to $F[x]$ is linear.
answer: Linear.

solutions.title: Check additivity and homogeneity
solutions.body:
Evaluation at $1$ is linear, so
$$f_2(\alpha a+\beta b)=\alpha a+\beta b+\big(\alpha a(1)+\beta b(1)\big)x^{N+1}=\alpha f_2(a)+\beta f_2(b).$$
So $f_2$ is linear (as a map into $F[x]$). $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 1.2.1(iii).** Fix $N\in\mathbb N$ and let $F_N$ be the space of polynomials $a(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{N}a_nx^n$ over $F$ (degree at most $N$). Determine with proof whether the map $a(x)\mapsto \sum_{n=0}^{N}(a_n-a_{N-n})x^n$ from $F_N$ to $F[x]$ is linear.
answer: Linear.

solutions.title: Check additivity and homogeneity
solutions.body: The $n$th coefficient of $f_3(\alpha a+\beta b)$ is $(\alpha a_n+\beta b_n)-(\alpha a_{N-n}+\beta b_{N-n})=\alpha(a_n-a_{N-n})+\beta(b_n-b_{N-n})$, which is the $n$th coefficient of $\alpha f_3(a)+\beta f_3(b)$. So $f_3$ is linear. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 1.2.2.** Describe as precisely as possible all inner products on $\mathbb C^2$. (An inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V^2\to\mathbb C$ satisfies $\langle x,y\rangle=\overline{\langle y,x\rangle}$, $\langle cx,y\rangle=c\langle x,y\rangle$, $\langle x,z\rangle+\langle y,z\rangle=\langle x+y,z\rangle$, and $\langle x,x\rangle>0$ for $x\ne0$.)
answer: $\langle u,v\rangle=r_1u_1\bar v_1+c\,u_1\bar v_2+\bar c\,u_2\bar v_1+r_2u_2\bar v_2$ with $r_1,r_2>0$, $c\in\mathbb C$ and $r_1r_2>|c|^2$ (i.e. $u^T H\bar v$ with $H$ Hermitian positive definite).

solutions.title: Expand in the standard basis
solutions.body:
Let $e_1=(1,0)$, $e_2=(0,1)$ and $h_{ij}=\langle e_i,e_j\rangle$. By linearity in the first slot and conjugate-linearity in the second (which follows from the axioms), for $u=(u_1,u_2)$, $v=(v_1,v_2)$,
$$\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_{i,j}h_{ij}u_i\bar v_j .$$
Conjugate symmetry gives $h_{11}=r_1$ and $h_{22}=r_2$ real, and $h_{21}=\overline{h_{12}}$. Put $c=h_{12}$. Positivity of $\langle e_i,e_i\rangle$ gives $r_1,r_2>0$.

**Positive definiteness.** $\langle u,u\rangle=r_1|u_1|^2+r_2|u_2|^2+2\operatorname{Re}(c\,u_1\bar u_2)$. Completing the square, with $u_2\neq 0$ and $t=u_1/u_2$,
$$\frac{\langle u,u\rangle}{|u_2|^2}=r_1\Big|t+\frac{\bar c}{r_1}\Big|^2+r_2-\frac{|c|^2}{r_1}$$.
The minimum over $t$ is $r_2-|c|^2/r_1$, so this is positive for all $t$ iff $r_1r_2>|c|^2$; and for $u_2=0$, $u_1\ne0$ it is $r_1|u_1|^2>0$.

So the inner products are exactly those given by a Hermitian matrix $H=\begin{pmatrix}r_1&c\\ \bar c&r_2\end{pmatrix}$ with $r_1>0$, $r_2>0$ and $r_1r_2>|c|^2$; each such $H$ satisfies all axioms. $\blacksquare$

reviewNote: The official solution gives r1,r2>0 and c nonzero but omits the necessary and sufficient condition r1*r2>|c|^2 (and c=0 is allowed); the stored answer includes it.

prompt: **Problem 1.2.3.** Show that if $\varphi:V\to W$ is an isomorphism of vector spaces (a bijective linear map), then $\varphi^{-1}$ is also an isomorphism.
answer: $\varphi^{-1}$ is bijective and linear.

solutions.title: Check linearity of the inverse
solutions.body:
$\varphi^{-1}$ exists and is bijective since $\varphi$ is. For $w_1,w_2\in W$ and scalars $a,b$ let $v_i=\varphi^{-1}(w_i)$. Then $\varphi(av_1+bv_2)=aw_1+bw_2$ by linearity of $\varphi$, so applying $\varphi^{-1}$,
$$\varphi^{-1}(aw_1+bw_2)=av_1+bv_2=a\varphi^{-1}(w_1)+b\varphi^{-1}(w_2).$$
Thus $\varphi^{-1}$ is a bijective linear map, i.e. an isomorphism. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 1.3.1.** Is matrix multiplication associative? Is it commutative? Explain why or why not.
answer: Associative: yes. Commutative: no.

solutions.title: Compose linear maps
solutions.body:
A matrix is the same as a linear map, and the product corresponds to composition (Problem 1.3.3). Composition of functions is associative: $((AB)C)v=A(B(Cv))=(A(BC))v$ for every $v$, so $(AB)C=A(BC)$.

It is not commutative: with $E_{12}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $E_{21}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$,
$$E_{12}E_{21}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\neq\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}=E_{21}E_{12}.$$
(Even the products may have different sizes when the factors are not square.)

prompt: **Problem 1.3.2.** Let $T_1,T_2:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ be linear maps with $n\times m$ matrices $\{a_{i,j}\}$ and $\{b_{i,j}\}$ (with respect to fixed bases). Show that $T_1+T_2$ has matrix $\{a_{i,j}+b_{i,j}\}$.
answer: The $j$th column of the matrix of $T_1+T_2$ is the sum of the $j$th columns.

solutions.title: Look at the images of basis vectors
solutions.body:
Let $v_1,\dots,v_m$ and $w_1,\dots,w_n$ be the bases. The $j$th column of a matrix lists the coordinates of the image of $v_j$: $T_1v_j=\sum_i a_{i,j}w_i$ and $T_2v_j=\sum_i b_{i,j}w_i$. Then
$$(T_1+T_2)v_j=T_1v_j+T_2v_j=\sum_i(a_{i,j}+b_{i,j})w_i,$$
so the $j$th column of $T_1+T_2$ is $(a_{i,j}+b_{i,j})_i$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 1.3.3.** Let $T_2:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ and $T_1:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p$ be linear maps given by matrices (with the product defined as in the text: $(AB)_{i,j}$ is the dot product of the $i$th row of $A$ with the $j$th column of $B$). Show that $T_1(T_2v)=(T_1T_2)v$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^m$, i.e. the matrix of the composite is the product of the matrices.
answer: Composition of maps corresponds to the matrix product.

solutions.title: Compute coordinates
solutions.body:
Let $A=(a_{k,i})$ be the $p\times n$ matrix of $T_1$ and $B=(b_{i,j})$ the $n\times m$ matrix of $T_2$. For $v=\sum_j v_je_j$, linearity gives $T_2v=\sum_j v_j T_2e_j=\sum_i\big(\sum_j b_{i,j}v_j\big)e_i$. Applying $T_1$,
$$T_1(T_2v)=\sum_i\Big(\sum_j b_{i,j}v_j\Big)T_1e_i=\sum_k\Big(\sum_j\Big(\sum_i a_{k,i}b_{i,j}\Big)v_j\Big)e_k .$$
The inner sum $\sum_i a_{k,i}b_{i,j}$ is the $(k,j)$ entry of $AB$ (row $k$ of $A$ dotted with column $j$ of $B$). So $T_1(T_2v)=(AB)v$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 2.1.1.** Let $M$ be a linear map of $V$ and $V_\lambda=\{v\in V: Mv=\lambda v\}$. Show that $V_\lambda$ is a subspace of $V$.
answer: $V_\lambda$ is closed under linear combinations and contains $0$.

solutions.title: Check closure
solutions.body: $0\in V_\lambda$. If $v,w\in V_\lambda$ and $a,b\in F$ then $M(av+bw)=aMv+bMw=a\lambda v+b\lambda w=\lambda(av+bw)$, so $av+bw\in V_\lambda$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 2.1.2.** Why does any linear map $M$ of a finite-dimensional vector space $V$ have only finitely many distinct eigenvalues?
answer: Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent, so there are at most $\dim V$ eigenvalues.

solutions.title: Independence of eigenvectors
solutions.body:
**Claim.** Eigenvectors $v_1,\dots,v_k$ with pairwise distinct eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k$ are linearly independent.

Induct on $k$; $k=1$ is clear since $v_1\ne0$. If $\sum c_iv_i=0$, apply $M-\lambda_k$ to get $\sum_{i<k}c_i(\lambda_i-\lambda_k)v_i=0$. By induction $c_i(\lambda_i-\lambda_k)=0$, so $c_i=0$ for $i<k$, and then $c_kv_k=0$ gives $c_k=0$.

If $M$ had more than $\dim V$ distinct eigenvalues, we would get more than $\dim V$ independent vectors, contradicting that any spanning set of size $\dim V$ bounds the size of independent sets (Problem 1.1.1). Hence at most $\dim V$ eigenvalues. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 2.1.3.** Let $M:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ be the linear map with matrix $\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\1&7\end{pmatrix}$. Find every eigenvector and the corresponding eigenvalue of $M$.
answer: Eigenvalue $2$: eigenvectors $t(-5,1)$, $t\neq 0$. Eigenvalue $7$: eigenvectors $t(0,1)$, $t\neq0$.

solutions.title: Solve $Mv=cv$
solutions.body:
$M(x,y)=(2x,\;x+7y)$. We need $2x=cx$ and $x+7y=cy$ with $(x,y)\ne0$.

- If $x\neq0$ then $c=2$, and $x+7y=2y$ gives $x=-5y$. Eigenvectors: $t(-5,1)$, $t\ne0$, eigenvalue $2$.
- If $x=0$ then $y\neq0$ and $7y=cy$ gives $c=7$. Eigenvectors: $t(0,1)$, $t\neq0$, eigenvalue $7$.

Check: $M(-5,1)=(-10,2)=2(-5,1)$ and $M(0,1)=(0,7)$. These are all eigenvectors. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 2.1.4.** For each of the linear maps from Problem 1.2.1, determine its eigenvalues and classify as well as you can the corresponding eigenvectors. The maps are defined on polynomials $a(x)=\sum_{n=0}^Na_nx^n$ of degree at most $N$: $f_1(a)=a(x)+a(1)$; $f_2(a)=a(x)+a(1)x^{N+1}$; $f_3(a)=\sum_{n=0}^N(a_n-a_{N-n})x^n$.
answer: $f_1$: eigenvalue $1$ (polynomials with $a(1)=0$) and $2$ (nonzero constants). $f_2$: only eigenvalue $1$ (polynomials with $a(1)=0$). $f_3$: eigenvalue $0$ (palindromic: $a_n=a_{N-n}$) and $2$ (antipalindromic: $a_n=-a_{N-n}$).

solutions.title: Solve $f(a)=\lambda a$
solutions.body:
**$f_1$.** $f_1(a)=\lambda a$ means $(\lambda-1)a(x)=a(1)$, a constant. If $\lambda=1$, this says $a(1)=0$: the eigenspace is $\{a:a(1)=0\}$ (sum of coefficients $0$). If $\lambda\neq1$ then $a$ is a constant $c\neq0$, and $(\lambda-1)c=c$ gives $\lambda=2$; eigenspace = constants.

**$f_2$.** $f_2(a)=\lambda a$ means $(\lambda-1)a=a(1)x^{N+1}$. The left side has degree $\le N$, so $a(1)=0$ and then $(\lambda-1)a=0$, forcing $\lambda=1$. Eigenspace: $\{a:a(1)=0\}$.

**$f_3$.** Let $\tilde a=\sum a_{N-n}x^n$ be the reversal; $f_3(a)=a-\tilde a$. If $a-\tilde a=\lambda a$ then $\tilde a=(1-\lambda)a$; reversing again, $a=(1-\lambda)\tilde a=(1-\lambda)^2a$, so $(1-\lambda)^2=1$, $\lambda\in\{0,2\}$. For $\lambda=0$: $\tilde a=a$ (palindromic polynomials, dimension $\lfloor N/2\rfloor+1$). For $\lambda=2$: $\tilde a=-a$ (antipalindromic, dimension $\lfloor (N+1)/2\rfloor$). $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 2.2.1.** Let $\mathfrak{sl}_n$ be the set of $n\times n$ complex matrices of trace $0$. What is $\dim\mathfrak{sl}_n$? Find a basis.
answer: $n^2-1$; basis $e_{i,j}$ ($i\neq j$) together with $e_{i,i}-e_{i+1,i+1}$ ($1\le i\le n-1$).

solutions.title: Count free entries
solutions.body:
The trace is a linear functional $\mathfrak{gl}_n\to\mathbb C$, nonzero (e.g. $\operatorname{tr}e_{1,1}=1$), so its kernel $\mathfrak{sl}_n$ has dimension $n^2-1$.

Explicit basis: the $n^2-n$ matrices $e_{i,j}$ with $i\neq j$ (a $1$ in row $i$, column $j$) and the $n-1$ matrices $h_i=e_{i,i}-e_{i+1,i+1}$, $1\le i\le n-1$. They lie in $\mathfrak{sl}_n$ and are independent. They span: a trace-zero matrix $X$ equals $\sum_{i\ne j}x_{ij}e_{ij}+\sum_i x_{ii}e_{ii}$, and since $\sum x_{ii}=0$ we have $\sum_ix_{ii}e_{ii}=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}(x_{11}+\dots+x_{ii})h_i$. Total $n^2-1$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 2.2.2.** Let $R_{2n}=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$, $R_{2n+1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&R_{2n}\end{pmatrix}$, $\tilde R_{2n}=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\-I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$. Let $\mathfrak{so}_m=\{M\in\mathfrak{gl}_m: M^TR_m+R_mM=0\}$ and $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}=\{M\in\mathfrak{gl}_{2n}:M^T\tilde R_{2n}+\tilde R_{2n}M=0\}$. Describe the elements of $\mathfrak{so}_m$ and $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}$ as precisely as you can and find $\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n}$, $\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}$, $\dim\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}$.
answer: $\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n}=2n^2-n$, $\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}=2n^2+n$, $\dim\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}=2n^2+n$.

solutions.title: Block computation
solutions.body:
Write $X=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}$ with $n\times n$ blocks.

**$\mathfrak{so}_{2n}$.** $X^TR_{2n}=\begin{pmatrix}C^T&A^T\\D^T&B^T\end{pmatrix}$ and $R_{2n}X=\begin{pmatrix}C&D\\A&B\end{pmatrix}$. The sum vanishes iff $C^T=-C$, $B^T=-B$, $D=-A^T$. So
$$X=\begin{pmatrix}M&P\\Q&-M^T\end{pmatrix},\quad M\text{ arbitrary},\ P,Q\text{ skew-symmetric}.$$
Dimension: $n^2+2\cdot\frac{n(n-1)}2=2n^2-n$.

**$\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}$.** $X^T\tilde R_{2n}=\begin{pmatrix}-C^T&A^T\\-D^T&B^T\end{pmatrix}$, $\tilde R_{2n}X=\begin{pmatrix}C&D\\-A&-B\end{pmatrix}$; the sum vanishes iff $C=C^T$, $B=B^T$, $D=-A^T$:
$$X=\begin{pmatrix}M&P\\Q&-M^T\end{pmatrix},\quad M\text{ arbitrary},\ P,Q\text{ symmetric}.$$
Dimension: $n^2+2\cdot\frac{n(n+1)}2=2n^2+n$.

**$\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}$.** Write $X=\begin{pmatrix}a&u^T\\w&Y\end{pmatrix}$ with $a$ a scalar, $u,w\in\mathbb C^{2n}$. Then $X^TR_{2n+1}+R_{2n+1}X=\begin{pmatrix}2a&w^TR_{2n}+u^T\\ u+R_{2n}w&Y^TR_{2n}+R_{2n}Y\end{pmatrix}$, so $a=0$, $u=-R_{2n}w$ and $Y\in\mathfrak{so}_{2n}$. Thus $w\in\mathbb C^{2n}$ is free and $Y\in\mathfrak{so}_{2n}$: dimension $2n+(2n^2-n)=2n^2+n$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 2.3.1.** Show that if $X$ and $Y$ are $n\times n$ complex matrices that commute and $X$ is nilpotent, then $\operatorname{tr}(XY)=0$.
answer: $XY$ is nilpotent, hence has all eigenvalues $0$ and trace $0$.

solutions.title: Nilpotent implies trace zero
solutions.body: If $X^k=0$ and $XY=YX$ then $(XY)^k=X^kY^k=0$, so $XY$ is nilpotent. If $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of a nilpotent $N$ with $N^k=0$ and eigenvector $v$, then $0=N^kv=\lambda^kv$, so $\lambda=0$. Over $\mathbb C$ the trace is the sum of the eigenvalues (counted with multiplicity: triangularize $N$; its diagonal consists of the eigenvalues). Hence $\operatorname{tr}(XY)=0$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 3.1.1.** Let $[f,g]=f\circ g-g\circ f$ for $f,g\in\mathfrak{gl}_n$. Show that the Jacobi identity holds, and therefore that $\mathfrak{gl}_n$ is a Lie algebra.
answer: Expand the three double brackets; the terms cancel in pairs.

solutions.title: Expand
solutions.body:
Bilinearity is clear, and $[f,f]=ff-ff=0$. Expanding,
$$[f,[g,h]]=fgh-fhg-ghf+hgf,$$
$$[g,[h,f]]=ghf-gfh-hfg+fhg,$$
$$[h,[f,g]]=hfg-hgf-fgh+gfh.$$
Adding: $fgh$ cancels $-fgh$, $-fhg$ cancels $fhg$, $-ghf$ cancels $ghf$, $hgf$ cancels $-hgf$, $-gfh$ cancels $gfh$, $-hfg$ cancels $hfg$. The sum is $0$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 3.1.2.** Explain why two Lie algebras of different dimension cannot be isomorphic.
answer: An isomorphism is in particular a linear bijection, which preserves dimension.

solutions.title: Use the vector space structure
solutions.body: A Lie algebra isomorphism is a bijective homomorphism, in particular a bijective linear map of the underlying vector spaces. It maps a basis to a basis (independence and spanning are preserved), so the dimensions agree. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 3.1.3.** Show that two (finite-dimensional) abelian Lie algebras $L_1,L_2$ are isomorphic if and only if they have the same dimension.
answer: Any linear isomorphism between abelian Lie algebras preserves the (zero) bracket.

solutions.title: Both directions
solutions.body: ($\Rightarrow$) Problem 3.1.2. ($\Leftarrow$) If $\dim L_1=\dim L_2$, there is a linear isomorphism $\varphi:L_1\to L_2$ (send a basis to a basis). For $x,y\in L_1$: $\varphi([x,y])=\varphi(0)=0=[\varphi(x),\varphi(y)]$, since both brackets vanish identically. So $\varphi$ is a bijective homomorphism. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 3.1.4.** In a Lie algebra $L$, assume $[x,[y,z]]=[[x,y],z]$ for all $x,y,z\in L$. What is the most general statement you can make about elements of $L$?
answer: The assumption holds iff $[x,[y,z]]=0$ for all $x,y,z$, i.e. $[L,L]\subseteq Z(L)$ (the center).

solutions.title: Use the Jacobi identity
solutions.body:
By hypothesis $[y,[z,x]]=[[y,z],x]=-[x,[y,z]]$. So in the Jacobi identity the first two terms cancel, leaving $[z,[x,y]]=0$ for all $x,y,z$. Thus every commutator $[x,y]$ lies in the center $Z(L)=\{c:[c,w]=0\ \forall w\in L\}$: $[L,L]\subseteq Z(L)$. Also $[[x,y],z]=-[z,[x,y]]=0$.

Conversely, if $[L,[L,L]]=0$ then both sides of the hypothesis vanish. So the hypothesis is **equivalent** to $[L,L]\subseteq Z(L)$, the strongest possible statement. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 3.1.5(i).** Let $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ have basis $v_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, $v_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $v_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ with bracket $[A,B]=AB-BA$, so $[v_3,v_1]=2v_1$, $[v_3,v_2]=-2v_2$, $[v_1,v_2]=v_3$. Suppose $\varphi:\mathfrak{sl}_2\to S$ is a bijective Lie algebra homomorphism onto a subalgebra $S\subseteq\mathfrak{gl}_n$ (bracket $XY-YX$), put $V_i=\varphi(v_i)$, and let $\lambda_3$ and $\lambda_3'$ be the greatest and least eigenvalue of $V_3$ (eigenvalues ordered by real part). Let $v,v'\in\mathbb C^n$ satisfy $V_3v=\lambda_3v$ and $V_3v'=\lambda_3'v'$. Find, with proof, $V_1v$ and $V_2v'$.

solutions.title: Shift eigenvalues
solutions.body:
Applying $\varphi$ to $[v_3,v_1]=2v_1$ gives $V_3V_1-V_1V_3=2V_1$. Hence
$$V_3(V_1v)=V_1V_3v+2V_1v=(\lambda_3+2)V_1v.$$
So $V_1v$ is either $0$ or an eigenvector of $V_3$ with eigenvalue $\lambda_3+2$, which has larger real part than the greatest eigenvalue: impossible. So $V_1v=0$.

Similarly $V_3V_2=V_2V_3-2V_2$ gives $V_3(V_2v')=(\lambda_3'-2)V_2v'$, and $\lambda_3'-2$ is below the least eigenvalue, so $V_2v'=0$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 3.1.5(ii).** Let $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ have basis $v_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, $v_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $v_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ with bracket $[A,B]=AB-BA$, so $[v_3,v_1]=2v_1$, $[v_3,v_2]=-2v_2$, $[v_1,v_2]=v_3$. Suppose $\varphi:\mathfrak{sl}_2\to S$ is a bijective Lie algebra homomorphism onto a subalgebra $S\subseteq\mathfrak{gl}_n$ (bracket $XY-YX$), put $V_i=\varphi(v_i)$, and let $\lambda_3$ and $\lambda_3'$ be the greatest and least eigenvalue of $V_3$ (eigenvalues ordered by real part). Let $v,v'\in\mathbb C^n$ satisfy $V_3v=\lambda_3v$ and $V_3v'=\lambda_3'v'$. Find, with proof, $\lambda_3$ and $\lambda_3'$. (You may use that $V_1v=0$ and $V_2v'=0$.)
answer: $\lambda_3=m$ is a nonnegative integer and $\lambda_3'=-m$.

solutions.title: A string of eigenvectors
solutions.body:
The relations are $[V_3,V_1]=2V_1$, $[V_3,V_2]=-2V_2$, $[V_1,V_2]=V_3$. Let $\lambda=\lambda_3$ and $w_k=V_2^kv$.

- $V_3w_k=(\lambda-2k)w_k$ (induction, using $V_3V_2=V_2V_3-2V_2$).
- $V_1w_k=k(\lambda-k+1)w_{k-1}$ (with $w_{-1}=0$). Induction: $V_1w_0=0$ and $V_1w_{k+1}=V_1V_2w_k=V_2V_1w_k+V_3w_k=\big(k(\lambda-k+1)+\lambda-2k\big)w_k=(k+1)(\lambda-k)w_k$.

Nonzero $w_k$ have distinct eigenvalues, so are independent; as $\mathbb C^n$ is finite-dimensional there is a smallest $m\ge0$ with $w_{m+1}=0$, and $w_m\ne0$. Then $0=V_1w_{m+1}=(m+1)(\lambda-m)w_m$ gives $\lambda=m\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$. Moreover $w_m\neq0$ is an eigenvector of $V_3$ with eigenvalue $\lambda-2m=-\lambda$, so $\lambda_3'\le-\lambda_3$.

**Reverse inequality.** The matrices $V_1'=V_2$, $V_2'=V_1$, $V_3'=-V_3$ satisfy the same three relations. The greatest eigenvalue of $V_3'$ is $-\lambda_3'$, with eigenvector $v'$ and $V_1'v'=V_2v'=0$. The argument above applied to $V'$ shows that the least eigenvalue of $V_3'$, namely $-\lambda_3$, satisfies $-\lambda_3\le-(-\lambda_3')$, i.e. $\lambda_3'\ge-\lambda_3$.

Hence $\lambda_3'=-\lambda_3$, with $\lambda_3=m$ a nonnegative integer. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 3.1.6.** A *Lie algebra* is a complex vector space $L$ with a bilinear bracket $[\cdot,\cdot]:L\times L\to L$ such that $[x,x]=0$ and the Jacobi identity $[x,[y,z]]+[y,[z,x]]+[z,[x,y]]=0$ holds. Up to isomorphism, how many Lie algebras have dimension $1$? dimension $2$? List them all.
answer: Dimension 1: one (abelian). Dimension 2: two, the abelian one and the one with basis $x,y$ and $[x,y]=x$.

solutions.title: Classify by the bracket of a basis
solutions.body:
**Dimension 1.** Elements are $ax$; $[ax,bx]=ab[x,x]=0$. So $L$ is abelian, and unique up to isomorphism by Problem 3.1.3.

**Dimension 2.** Let $e,f$ be a basis. By bilinearity and $[e,e]=[f,f]=0$, $[ae+bf,ce+df]=(ad-bc)[e,f]$, so everything is determined by $[e,f]$.

- If $[e,f]=0$, $L$ is abelian (unique by 3.1.3).
- If $[e,f]=c\neq0$, take $x=c$ and $y$ any vector independent of $x$. Then $[x,y]=\mu[e,f]$ with $\mu=\det\neq0$ (change of basis), so $[x,y]=\mu c=\mu x$ with $\mu\ne0$. Replacing $y$ by $y/\mu$ gives $[x,y]=x$.

Any two algebras of the second kind are isomorphic via $x\mapsto x'$, $y\mapsto y'$, and the two kinds are not isomorphic (one is abelian, the other not). So: 1 algebra in dimension 1 and 2 in dimension 2. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 3.2.1(i).** A *subalgebra* $S$ of a Lie algebra $L$ is a subspace with $[x,y]\in S$ for $x,y\in S$; an *ideal* $I$ is a subalgebra with $[x,y]\in I$ for $x\in I$, $y\in L$. If $L$ is an abelian Lie algebra, show that any subspace of $L$ is a subalgebra and an ideal.
answer: All brackets are $0$, which lies in every subspace.

solutions.title: Brackets vanish
solutions.body: For a subspace $W\subseteq L$, $x\in W$, $y\in L$: $[x,y]=0\in W$. So $W$ is an ideal, and in particular a subalgebra. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 3.2.1(ii).** A *subalgebra* of a Lie algebra $L$ is a subspace $S$ with $[x,y]\in S$ for all $x,y\in S$; an *ideal* $I$ is a subalgebra with $[x,y]\in I$ for $x\in I$, $y\in L$. Find a nonabelian Lie algebra of $n\times n$ matrices for some $n>2$ (bracket $XY-YX$) that has a subalgebra that is not an ideal. Specify the subalgebra and briefly justify why it is not an ideal.
answer: $L=\mathfrak{gl}_3$ with the diagonal matrices as subalgebra.

solutions.title: Diagonal matrices in gl_3
solutions.body:
Let $L=\mathfrak{gl}_3$ (nonabelian: $[e_{12},e_{21}]\neq0$) and $S$ the diagonal matrices. Diagonal matrices commute, so $[S,S]=0\subseteq S$ and $S$ is a subalgebra. It is not an ideal: with $x=e_{11}\in S$ and $y=e_{12}\in L$,
$$[x,y]=e_{11}e_{12}-e_{12}e_{11}=e_{12}\notin S.$$ $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 3.2.2.** Let $L$ be a subspace of $\mathfrak{gl}_n$ and $I=\{x\in L: x\text{ nilpotent}\}$. Is $I$ a subalgebra? an ideal? Fully justify your responses.
answer: In general neither: e.g. for $L=\mathfrak{sl}_2$ the nilpotent matrices $e_{12},e_{21}$ have bracket $\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$, which is not nilpotent.

solutions.title: Counterexample
solutions.body: Take $L=\mathfrak{sl}_2$. The matrices $e=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $f=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ satisfy $e^2=f^2=0$, so $e,f\in I$. But $[e,f]=h=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$, and $h^k=\operatorname{diag}(1,(-1)^k)\ne0$ for all $k$, so $h\notin I$. Thus $I$ is not closed under the bracket: not a subalgebra, and hence not an ideal (an ideal is a subalgebra). For general $n$ embed this in the upper left $2\times2$ block, or use $e_{1,2}$ and $e_{2,1}$ in $L=\mathfrak{sl}_n$. (Sometimes $I$ is both, e.g. if $L$ consists of strictly upper triangular matrices, so the statement is false in general rather than in every case.) $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 3.2.3.** For subspaces $L_1,L_2$ of a Lie algebra $L$ let $[L_1,L_2]$ denote the span of all brackets $[v_1,v_2]$, $v_i\in L_i$. Is $[I,J]$ an ideal of $L$ for ideals $I,J$ of $L$?
answer: Yes (with $[I,J]$ the span of the brackets).

solutions.title: Use the Jacobi identity
solutions.body: Let $x\in I$, $y\in J$, $z\in L$. By Jacobi, $[[x,y],z]=-[[y,z],x]-[[z,x],y]$. Here $[y,z]\in J$ and $[z,x]\in I$ because $J,I$ are ideals, so $[[y,z],x]$ and $[[z,x],y]$ are brackets of an element of $I$ with an element of $J$, hence in $[I,J]$. So $[[x,y],z]\in[I,J]$. By linearity, $[a,z]\in[I,J]$ for every $a$ in the span $[I,J]$ and $z\in L$. Taking $z\in[I,J]$ shows it is a subalgebra, so $[I,J]$ is an ideal. $\blacksquare$

reviewNote: Taken literally, the printed set {[v1,v2]} of single brackets need not be closed under addition (for a free 2-step nilpotent Lie algebra on 4 generators, x1x2+x3x4 is not a single commutator); the answer uses the span, as in the official solution.

prompt: **Problem 3.2.4.** Let $\varphi:L_1\to L_2$ be a Lie algebra homomorphism. Show that $\ker\varphi$ is an ideal of $L_1$ and $\operatorname{im}\varphi$ is a subalgebra of $L_2$.
answer: Compute $\varphi$ of brackets.

solutions.title: Direct check
solutions.body:
Both $\ker\varphi$ and $\operatorname{im}\varphi$ are subspaces since $\varphi$ is linear.

**Kernel.** If $x\in\ker\varphi$ and $y\in L_1$, then $\varphi([x,y])=[\varphi(x),\varphi(y)]=[0,\varphi(y)]=0$, so $[x,y]\in\ker\varphi$. Hence $\ker\varphi$ is an ideal (and in particular a subalgebra).

**Image.** If $a=\varphi(x)$, $b=\varphi(y)$ then $[a,b]=\varphi([x,y])\in\operatorname{im}\varphi$. So $\operatorname{im}\varphi$ is a subalgebra of $L_2$ (it inherits the Jacobi identity). $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 3.3.1(i).** Let $V_d$ be the real vector space of polynomials of degree at most $d$ (with real coefficients). Find $\dim V_3$ and a basis.

solutions.title: Monomials
solutions.body: Every element of $V_3$ is uniquely $a+bx+cx^2+dx^3$, so $\{1,x,x^2,x^3\}$ spans and is independent (a polynomial that is zero has all coefficients zero). Hence $\dim V_3=4$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 3.3.1(ii).** On the space $V_2$ of real polynomials $p=\alpha_0+\alpha_1x+\alpha_2x^2$ of degree at most $2$ define the bracket $[p,q]=(\alpha_1\beta_2-\alpha_2\beta_1)+(\alpha_2\beta_0-\alpha_0\beta_2)x+(\alpha_0\beta_1-\alpha_1\beta_0)x^2$ for $q=\beta_0+\beta_1x+\beta_2x^2$ (this is a Lie algebra). Find a subspace $S$ of $\mathfrak{gl}_n$ for some $n$ and an explicit isomorphism $V_2\to S$ preserving the bracket (where $\mathfrak{gl}_n$ has bracket $XY-YX$).
answer: $n=3$: $p\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}0&-\alpha_2&\alpha_1\\ \alpha_2&0&-\alpha_0\\ -\alpha_1&\alpha_0&0\end{pmatrix}$, onto the skew-symmetric matrices.

solutions.title: Cross product as commutator
solutions.body:
The bracket is the cross product of the coefficient vectors $a=(\alpha_0,\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$, $b=(\beta_0,\beta_1,\beta_2)$: $[p,q]\leftrightarrow a\times b$. For $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)$ let
$$A_u=\begin{pmatrix}0&-u_3&u_2\\u_3&0&-u_1\\-u_2&u_1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\text{so }A_uw=u\times w.$$
The map $u\mapsto A_u$ is linear and injective, and its image is the space $S$ of skew-symmetric $3\times3$ matrices. By the Jacobi identity for the cross product, $[A_u,A_v]w=u\times(v\times w)-v\times(u\times w)=(u\times v)\times w$, so $[A_u,A_v]=A_{u\times v}$. Hence $\varphi(p)=A_{(\alpha_0,\alpha_1,\alpha_2)}$ is a bracket-preserving linear bijection $V_2\to S$:
$$\varphi(p)=\begin{pmatrix}0&-\alpha_2&\alpha_1\\ \alpha_2&0&-\alpha_0\\ -\alpha_1&\alpha_0&0\end{pmatrix}.$$ $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 3.3.2.** Let $\mathbb R^2$ be given the abelian Lie bracket $[x,y]=0$. Find a subspace $S$ of $\mathfrak{gl}_n$ for some $n$ and an explicit isomorphism $\mathbb R^2\to S$ of Lie algebras (bracket $XY-YX$ on $\mathfrak{gl}_n$).
answer: $n=2$: $(a,b)\mapsto\operatorname{diag}(a,b)$, onto the diagonal matrices.

solutions.title: Diagonal matrices
solutions.body: Let $S$ be the diagonal $2\times2$ matrices and $\varphi(a,b)=\begin{pmatrix}a&0\\0&b\end{pmatrix}$. It is a linear bijection onto $S$. Diagonal matrices commute, so $[\varphi(x),\varphi(y)]=0=\varphi([x,y])$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 3.4.1.** For $x$ in a Lie algebra $L$, the adjoint map is $\operatorname{ad}x:L\to L$, $(\operatorname{ad}x)(y)=[x,y]$. Verify that $\operatorname{ad}x$ is a linear map.
answer: $[x,\cdot]$ is linear by bilinearity of the bracket.

solutions.title: Bilinearity
solutions.body: For $y,z\in L$ and scalars $a,b$: $(\operatorname{ad}x)(ay+bz)=[x,ay+bz]=a[x,y]+b[x,z]=a(\operatorname{ad}x)(y)+b(\operatorname{ad}x)(z)$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 3.4.2(i).** For $x$ in a Lie algebra $L$, the adjoint map is $\operatorname{ad}x:L\to L$, $(\operatorname{ad}x)(y)=[x,y]$. $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ has basis $v_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, $v_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $v_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ with $[v_1,v_2]=v_3$, $[v_3,v_1]=2v_1$, $[v_3,v_2]=-2v_2$. Explain how $\operatorname{ad}x$ can be thought of as an element of $\mathfrak{gl}_3$ when $x\in\mathfrak{sl}_2$.
answer: $\operatorname{ad}x$ is a linear map of the 3-dimensional space $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ to itself, so after choosing a basis it is a $3\times3$ matrix.

solutions.title: Matrix of a linear map
solutions.body: $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ is $3$-dimensional with basis $v_1,v_2,v_3$. By Problem 3.4.1, $\operatorname{ad}x$ is a linear map $\mathfrak{sl}_2\to\mathfrak{sl}_2$. A linear map of a $3$-dimensional space to itself is represented, once an ordered basis is fixed, by a $3\times3$ matrix whose $j$th column holds the coordinates of $(\operatorname{ad}x)(v_j)$. That matrix is an element of $\mathfrak{gl}_3$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 3.4.2(ii).** For $x$ in a Lie algebra $L$, the adjoint map is $\operatorname{ad}x:L\to L$, $(\operatorname{ad}x)(y)=[x,y]$. $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ has basis $v_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, $v_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $v_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ with $[v_1,v_2]=v_3$, $[v_3,v_1]=2v_1$, $[v_3,v_2]=-2v_2$. Find an explicit, nontrivial isomorphism from $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ to a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{gl}_3$.
answer: $x\mapsto$ the matrix of $\operatorname{ad}x$ in the basis $(v_1,v_2,v_3)$; e.g. $v_1\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}0&0&-2\\0&0&0\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $v_2\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\0&0&2\\-1&0&0\end{pmatrix}$, $v_3\mapsto\operatorname{diag}(2,-2,0)$.

solutions.title: The adjoint representation
solutions.body:
Compute with the basis $(v_1,v_2,v_3)$; the columns are the images of $v_1,v_2,v_3$.

- $\operatorname{ad}v_1$: $v_1\mapsto0$, $v_2\mapsto[v_1,v_2]=v_3$, $v_3\mapsto[v_1,v_3]=-2v_1$. Matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&0&-2\\0&0&0\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix}$.
- $\operatorname{ad}v_2$: $v_1\mapsto[v_2,v_1]=-v_3$, $v_2\mapsto0$, $v_3\mapsto[v_2,v_3]=2v_2$. Matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\0&0&2\\-1&0&0\end{pmatrix}$.
- $\operatorname{ad}v_3$: $v_1\mapsto2v_1$, $v_2\mapsto-2v_2$, $v_3\mapsto0$. Matrix $\operatorname{diag}(2,-2,0)$.

Define $\rho(av_1+bv_2+cv_3)=a\operatorname{ad}v_1+b\operatorname{ad}v_2+c\operatorname{ad}v_3=\operatorname{ad}(av_1+bv_2+cv_3)$ (linear by Problem 3.4.1 and bilinearity).

**Homomorphism.** $\operatorname{ad}[x,y]=[\operatorname{ad}x,\operatorname{ad}y]$ because for all $z$, $[[x,y],z]=[x,[y,z]]-[y,[x,z]]$ (Jacobi).

**Injective.** The three matrices above are linearly independent (their nonzero entries sit in different positions, e.g. $\operatorname{ad}v_3$ is diagonal and nonzero, $\operatorname{ad}v_1$ has entries only at $(1,3),(3,2)$ and $\operatorname{ad}v_2$ only at $(2,3),(3,1)$). So $\rho$ is a bijection onto the span, which is a subalgebra (image of a homomorphism, Problem 3.2.4). Hence $\mathfrak{sl}_2\cong\operatorname{span}\{\operatorname{ad}v_1,\operatorname{ad}v_2,\operatorname{ad}v_3\}\subseteq\mathfrak{gl}_3$, and the isomorphism is nontrivial. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 3.4.3.** For $x$ in a Lie algebra $L$, the adjoint map is $\operatorname{ad}x:L\to L$, $(\operatorname{ad}x)(y)=[x,y]$. Show that the set $\mathfrak t_3$ of $3\times3$ complex upper-triangular matrices is a Lie algebra under $[X,Y]=XY-YX$. Find a basis $e_1,\dots,e_6$ and write $\operatorname{ad}e_i$ explicitly for each basis vector. Find the eigenvalues of each $\operatorname{ad}e_i$.
answer: Basis $E_{11},E_{22},E_{33},E_{12},E_{13},E_{23}$, $\dim 6$. $\operatorname{ad}E_{ii}$ are diagonal with eigenvalues in $\{0,\pm1\}$; $\operatorname{ad}E_{ij}$ ($i<j$) are nilpotent, all eigenvalues $0$.

solutions.title: Compute with matrix units
solutions.body:
**Lie algebra.** Upper-triangular matrices are closed under products, so under $XY-YX$; bracket is bilinear, $[X,X]=0$, and Jacobi holds as in 3.1.1 for matrices. The diagonal entries of $XY$ and $YX$ coincide, so in fact $[X,Y]$ is strictly upper triangular.

**Basis.** $E_{ij}$ for $i\le j$ (six matrices), ordered $E_{11},E_{22},E_{33},E_{12},E_{13},E_{23}$, $\dim=6$. Use $[E_{ij},E_{kl}]=\delta_{jk}E_{il}-\delta_{li}E_{kj}$.

**Adjoint maps** (we list the action on the basis; the matrix of $\operatorname{ad}e$ has as $j$th column the coordinates of $[e,e_j]$ in the order above; entries not listed are $0$).

- $\operatorname{ad}E_{11}$: $E_{12}\mapsto E_{12}$, $E_{13}\mapsto E_{13}$; all others $\mapsto0$. Diagonal $\operatorname{diag}(0,0,0,1,1,0)$.
- $\operatorname{ad}E_{22}$: $E_{12}\mapsto-E_{12}$, $E_{23}\mapsto E_{23}$. Diagonal $\operatorname{diag}(0,0,0,-1,0,1)$.
- $\operatorname{ad}E_{33}$: $E_{13}\mapsto-E_{13}$, $E_{23}\mapsto-E_{23}$. Diagonal $\operatorname{diag}(0,0,0,0,-1,-1)$.
- $\operatorname{ad}E_{12}$: $E_{11}\mapsto-E_{12}$, $E_{22}\mapsto E_{12}$, $E_{23}\mapsto E_{13}$; others $\mapsto 0$.
- $\operatorname{ad}E_{13}$: $E_{11}\mapsto-E_{13}$, $E_{33}\mapsto E_{13}$; others $\mapsto0$.
- $\operatorname{ad}E_{23}$: $E_{22}\mapsto-E_{23}$, $E_{33}\mapsto E_{23}$, $E_{12}\mapsto-E_{13}$; others $\mapsto0$.

**Eigenvalues.** The first three are diagonal in this basis, so their eigenvalues are the diagonal entries: $\{0,1\}$, $\{0,\pm1\}$, $\{0,-1\}$ respectively. Each of $E_{12},E_{13},E_{23}$ is a nilpotent matrix (its square is $0$), so by Problem 3.4.5 the maps $\operatorname{ad}E_{12},\operatorname{ad}E_{13},\operatorname{ad}E_{23}$ are nilpotent and all their eigenvalues are $0$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 3.4.4.** For $x$ in a Lie algebra $L$, the adjoint map is $\operatorname{ad}x:L\to L$, $(\operatorname{ad}x)(y)=[x,y]$. Show that $[x,y]=0$ implies $(\operatorname{ad}x)\circ(\operatorname{ad}y)=(\operatorname{ad}y)\circ(\operatorname{ad}x)$.
answer: Apply Jacobi to $x,y,z$.

solutions.title: Use Jacobi
solutions.body: For $z\in L$, Jacobi gives $[x,[y,z]]=-[y,[z,x]]-[z,[x,y]]=-[y,[z,x]]-0=[y,[x,z]]$ (using $[z,x]=-[x,z]$ from $[a+b,a+b]=0$). So $(\operatorname{ad}x\circ\operatorname{ad}y)(z)=(\operatorname{ad}y\circ\operatorname{ad}x)(z)$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 3.4.5.** For $x$ in a Lie algebra $L$, the adjoint map is $\operatorname{ad}x:L\to L$, $(\operatorname{ad}x)(y)=[x,y]$. Let $L\subseteq\mathfrak{gl}_n$ be a matrix Lie algebra. If $x$ is nilpotent, is $\operatorname{ad}x$ nilpotent? If $\operatorname{ad}x$ is nilpotent, is $x$ nilpotent? Justify.
answer: Yes; no (e.g. $x=I_n$ in $\mathfrak{gl}_n$, where $\operatorname{ad}I_n=0$).

solutions.title: Left minus right multiplication
solutions.body:
**First part.** Let $x^k=0$. On matrices write $\operatorname{ad}x=\lambda-\rho$ with $\lambda(y)=xy$, $\rho(y)=yx$; these commute and $\lambda^k=\rho^k=0$. By the binomial theorem,
$$(\operatorname{ad}x)^{2k-1}=\sum_{i+j=2k-1}(-1)^j\binom{2k-1}{j}\lambda^i\rho^j,$$
and in each term $i\ge k$ or $j\ge k$, so every term is $0$. Hence $\operatorname{ad}x$ is nilpotent (on $L$ too, being a restriction).

**Second part.** No. In $L=\mathfrak{gl}_n$, $x=I_n$ gives $(\operatorname{ad}I_n)(y)=y-y=0$, so $\operatorname{ad}I_n$ is nilpotent, but $I_n^k=I_n\ne0$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 3.4.6.** For $x$ in a Lie algebra $L$, the adjoint map is $\operatorname{ad}x:L\to L$, $(\operatorname{ad}x)(y)=[x,y]$. Show that $\operatorname{ad}x$ is a derivation: $(\operatorname{ad}x)([y,z])=[(\operatorname{ad}x)(y),z]+[y,(\operatorname{ad}x)(z)]$ for all $y,z$.
answer: This is the Jacobi identity rewritten.

solutions.title: Rewrite Jacobi
solutions.body: By Jacobi, $[x,[y,z]]=-[y,[z,x]]-[z,[x,y]]=[y,[x,z]]+[[x,y],z]$ (using anticommutativity). The right-hand side is $[y,(\operatorname{ad}x)z]+[(\operatorname{ad}x)y,z]$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 4.1.1.** For a Lie algebra $L$ the *Killing form* is $\kappa(x,y)=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{ad}x\circ\operatorname{ad}y)$. Verify that $\kappa$ is symmetric and bilinear.
answer: Linearity of $\operatorname{ad}$ and of trace, and $\operatorname{tr}(XY)=\operatorname{tr}(YX)$.

solutions.title: Direct verification
solutions.body: $\operatorname{ad}$ is linear in $x$ (bracket bilinear), $\circ$ is bilinear, and $\operatorname{tr}$ is linear. So $\kappa(ax+bx',y)=a\kappa(x,y)+b\kappa(x',y)$, and likewise in $y$. Symmetry: $\kappa(x,y)=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{ad}x\operatorname{ad}y)=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{ad}y\operatorname{ad}x)=\kappa(y,x)$ by $\operatorname{tr}(XY)=\operatorname{tr}(YX)$ (since $\sum_{i,j}X_{ij}Y_{ji}$ is symmetric in $X,Y$). $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 4.1.2.** With the Killing form $\kappa(x,y)=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{ad}x\circ\operatorname{ad}y)$, show that $\kappa([x,y],z)=\kappa(x,[y,z])$.
answer: Use $\operatorname{ad}[x,y]=[\operatorname{ad}x,\operatorname{ad}y]$ and $\operatorname{tr}(XY)=\operatorname{tr}(YX)$.

solutions.title: Trace manipulation
solutions.body:
By Jacobi, $\operatorname{ad}[x,y]=\operatorname{ad}x\operatorname{ad}y-\operatorname{ad}y\operatorname{ad}x$. Hence
$$\kappa([x,y],z)=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{ad}x\operatorname{ad}y\operatorname{ad}z)-\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{ad}y\operatorname{ad}x\operatorname{ad}z).$$
By cyclicity of the trace, $\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{ad}y\operatorname{ad}x\operatorname{ad}z)=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{ad}x\operatorname{ad}z\operatorname{ad}y)$. So
$$\kappa([x,y],z)=\operatorname{tr}\big(\operatorname{ad}x(\operatorname{ad}y\operatorname{ad}z-\operatorname{ad}z\operatorname{ad}y)\big)=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{ad}x\operatorname{ad}[y,z])=\kappa(x,[y,z]).$$ $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 4.1.3.** Let $L\subseteq\mathfrak{gl}_n$ be a Lie algebra whose Killing form is non-degenerate (a semisimple Lie algebra: $\kappa(x,y)=0$ for all $y$ implies $x=0$). Recall that a matrix is semisimple if it is diagonalizable. Show that $x\in L$ is semisimple if and only if $\operatorname{ad}x$ is semisimple (as a linear map $L\to L$).
answer: ($\Rightarrow$) $\operatorname{ad}x$ is diagonalizable on $\mathfrak{gl}_n$ and hence on the invariant subspace $L$. ($\Leftarrow$) Jordan decomposition $x=s+n$: $\operatorname{ad}n$ is nilpotent and semisimple, hence $0$, so $n$ is central, hence $0$ by non-degeneracy.

solutions.title: Both directions
solutions.body:
**($\Rightarrow$)** If $x$ is diagonalizable, choose a basis in which $x=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)$. In $\mathfrak{gl}_n$, $[x,e_{ij}]=(\lambda_i-\lambda_j)e_{ij}$, so $\operatorname{ad}x$ is diagonalizable on $\mathfrak{gl}_n$. The subspace $L$ is invariant under $\operatorname{ad}x$ (since $L$ is a subalgebra), and the restriction of a diagonalizable map to an invariant subspace is diagonalizable (its minimal polynomial divides one with distinct roots).

**($\Leftarrow$)** Write the Jordan decomposition $x=s+n$ in $\mathfrak{gl}_n$: $s$ diagonalizable, $n$ nilpotent, $sn=ns$, and $s,n$ are polynomials in $x$. By the first part and Problem 3.4.5, $\operatorname{ad}s$ is diagonalizable and $\operatorname{ad}n$ is nilpotent (on $\mathfrak{gl}_n$), they commute, and $\operatorname{ad}x=\operatorname{ad}s+\operatorname{ad}n$ is the Jordan decomposition of $\operatorname{ad}x$ on $\mathfrak{gl}_n$. Since $\operatorname{ad}s$ and $\operatorname{ad}n$ are polynomials in $\operatorname{ad}x$, $L$ is invariant under them, and they restrict to the Jordan decomposition of $\operatorname{ad}x|_L$. If $\operatorname{ad}x|_L$ is semisimple, uniqueness of the decomposition ($\operatorname{ad}x=\operatorname{ad}x+0$) gives $\operatorname{ad}n|_L=0$, i.e. $[n,y]=0$ for all $y\in L$. For a semisimple Lie algebra the Jordan components $s,n$ of an element of $L$ lie in $L$ (standard), so $n\in L$ and $\kappa(n,y)=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{ad}n\operatorname{ad}y)=0$ for all $y$; non-degeneracy gives $n=0$ and $x=s$ is semisimple. $\blacksquare$

reviewNote: The converse direction uses the standard (unproved here) fact that the semisimple and nilpotent Jordan parts of an element of a semisimple matrix Lie algebra lie in that algebra; the official solution is also only a sketch.

prompt: **Problem 4.1.4(i).** Let $L$ be a Lie algebra with Killing form $\kappa$ and $I\subseteq L$ an ideal. Let $I'=\{x\in L:\kappa(x,y)=0\ \forall y\in I\}$. Show that $I'$ is also an ideal.
answer: Use $\kappa([x,z],y)=\kappa(x,[z,y])$ and that $I$ is an ideal.

solutions.title: Invariance of the form
solutions.body: $I'$ is a subspace since $\kappa$ is bilinear. Let $x\in I'$, $z\in L$, $y\in I$. By Problem 4.1.2, $\kappa([x,z],y)=\kappa(x,[z,y])$, and $[z,y]\in I$ because $I$ is an ideal, so this is $0$. Hence $[x,z]\in I'$. Thus $I'$ is an ideal. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 4.1.4(ii).** Let $L$ be a Lie algebra with non-degenerate Killing form $\kappa$ (semisimple). A Lie algebra is *simple* if its only ideals are $\{0\}$ and itself. Show that $L=L_1\oplus\dots\oplus L_k$ (as Lie algebras, with $[L_i,L_j]=0$ for $i\ne j$) where each $L_i$ is a simple ideal of $L$.
answer: Split off a minimal ideal $I$ via $L=I\oplus I^\perp$ and induct on the dimension.

solutions.title: Induction on dimension
solutions.body:
If $L=0$ there is nothing to show. Otherwise let $I$ be a nonzero ideal of least dimension, and $I'=I^\perp$ (an ideal by part (i)).

**Step 0: $L$ has no nonzero abelian ideal.** If $A$ is an abelian ideal, $x\in A$, $y\in L$, then $(\operatorname{ad}x\operatorname{ad}y)^2(z)=[x,[y,[x,[y,z]]]]=0$, because $[y,[x,[y,z]]]\in A$ and $[x,A]=0$. So $\operatorname{ad}x\operatorname{ad}y$ is nilpotent, $\kappa(x,y)=0$ for all $y$, and $x=0$.

**Step 1: $I\cap I'=0$.** $J=I\cap I'$ is an ideal inside $I$, so by minimality $J=0$ or $J=I$. Suppose $J=I$, i.e. $\kappa(I,I)=0$. For $x\in I,y\in L$: $\operatorname{ad}x\operatorname{ad}y$ maps $L$ into $I$ and $\operatorname{ad} x\operatorname{ad}y|_I=\operatorname{ad}_Ix\circ\operatorname{ad}y|_I$, so $\kappa_L(x,y)=\operatorname{tr}_I(\operatorname{ad}x\operatorname{ad}y|_I)$; for $y\in I$ this is the Killing form of $I$, which is $0$. By Cartan's solvability criterion $I$ is solvable, so $[I,I]\subsetneq I$. $[I,I]$ is an ideal of $L$ (by Jacobi), so by minimality $[I,I]=0$: $I$ is abelian, contradicting Step 0. So $J=0$.

**Step 2: $L=I\oplus I'$.** $\dim I'\ge\dim L-\dim I$ (it is the kernel of the map $L\to I^*$, $x\mapsto\kappa(x,\cdot)|_I$) and $I\cap I'=0$, so $L=I\oplus I'$. Both are ideals, so $[I,I']\subseteq I\cap I'=0$.

**Step 3: $I$ is simple.** An ideal of $I$ is an ideal of $L$ (brackets with $I'$ vanish), so by minimality $I$ has only the ideals $0$ and $I$. Also $I$ is not abelian (Step 0), so it is a genuine simple Lie algebra.

**Step 4: induction.** $\kappa_L$ restricted to $I'$ equals $\kappa_{I'}$ (as $[I,I']=0$) and is non-degenerate since $\kappa_L(I,I')=0$ and $\kappa_L$ is non-degenerate on $L=I\oplus I'$. So $I'$ is semisimple of smaller dimension and decomposes by induction. $\blacksquare$

reviewNote: The proof cites Cartan's criterion (a Lie algebra with identically zero Killing form is solvable), which the paper does not prove; the official solution only sketches it.

prompt: **Problem 4.2.1.** Let $L$ be a Lie algebra with a maximal toral subalgebra $H$ (an abelian subalgebra of semisimple elements) such that $L$ has a basis of simultaneous eigenvectors of $\operatorname{ad}h$, $h\in H$: $[h,v_i]=\lambda_i(h)v_i$. Show that each $\lambda_i:H\to\mathbb C$ is linear.
answer: $h\mapsto[h,v_i]$ is linear.

solutions.title: Bilinearity of the bracket
solutions.body: For $h_1,h_2\in H$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$: $\lambda_i(\alpha h_1+\beta h_2)v_i=[\alpha h_1+\beta h_2,v_i]=\alpha[h_1,v_i]+\beta[h_2,v_i]=(\alpha\lambda_i(h_1)+\beta\lambda_i(h_2))v_i$. Since $v_i\ne0$, $\lambda_i(\alpha h_1+\beta h_2)=\alpha\lambda_i(h_1)+\beta\lambda_i(h_2)$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 4.2.2.** In the setting of a Lie algebra $L$ with maximal toral subalgebra $H$ and a basis of simultaneous eigenvectors of $\operatorname{ad}H$, let $L_\lambda=\{v\in L:[h,v]=\lambda(h)v\ \forall h\in H\}$ for $\lambda\in H^*$. Show that $L$ is isomorphic as a vector space to $\bigoplus_{\lambda}L_\lambda$ (the sum over those $\lambda$ with $L_\lambda\neq0$).
answer: $L=\sum L_\lambda$ because of the eigenbasis, and the sum is direct because eigenvectors for distinct functionals are independent.

solutions.title: Spanning and independence
solutions.body:
**Spanning.** Each basis vector $v_i$ lies in $L_{\lambda_i}$, so $L=\sum_\lambda L_\lambda$.

**Directness.** Suppose $\sum_{k=1}^mu_k=0$ with $u_k\in L_{\mu_k}$ for distinct $\mu_k$ and $m$ minimal with all $u_k\neq0$ ($m\ge2$). Pick $h\in H$ with $\mu_1(h)\ne\mu_2(h)$. Apply $\operatorname{ad}h-\mu_1(h)$: $\sum_{k\ge2}(\mu_k(h)-\mu_1(h))u_k=0$ is a shorter relation with $u_2$-coefficient nonzero, contradicting minimality. So the sum is direct and the map $\bigoplus L_\lambda\to L$, $(u_\lambda)\mapsto\sum u_\lambda$, is a linear isomorphism. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 4.2.3.** Let $L$ be a Lie algebra with non-degenerate Killing form $\kappa$, a maximal toral subalgebra $H$ and root space decomposition $L=\bigoplus_\lambda L_\lambda$ (with $L_0=H$). For roots $\alpha,\beta$, determine the condition on $\alpha$ and $\beta$ under which $\kappa(v_1,v_2)\neq0$ for some $v_1\in L_\alpha$, $v_2\in L_\beta$.
answer: $\kappa(L_\alpha,L_\beta)\ne0$ exactly when $\alpha+\beta=0$ (i.e. $\beta=-\alpha$).

solutions.title: Orthogonality of root spaces
solutions.body:
**Necessity.** Suppose $\alpha+\beta\ne0$; choose $h\in H$ with $(\alpha+\beta)(h)\neq0$. For $v_1\in L_\alpha,v_2\in L_\beta$, invariance (Problem 4.1.2) gives $\kappa([v_1,h],v_2)=\kappa(v_1,[h,v_2])$, i.e. $\kappa([h,v_1],v_2)=-\kappa(v_1,[h,v_2])$. Hence
$$\alpha(h)\kappa(v_1,v_2)=-\beta(h)\kappa(v_1,v_2),$$
so $(\alpha+\beta)(h)\kappa(v_1,v_2)=0$ and $\kappa(v_1,v_2)=0$.

**Sufficiency.** Let $\alpha$ be a root and $0\neq v_1\in L_\alpha$. By non-degeneracy there is $y\in L$ with $\kappa(v_1,y)\neq0$. Decompose $y=\sum y_\gamma$ with $y_\gamma\in L_\gamma$. By necessity, $\kappa(v_1,y_\gamma)=0$ unless $\gamma=-\alpha$, so $\kappa(v_1,y_{-\alpha})\ne0$; in particular $-\alpha$ is a root and $\kappa(L_\alpha,L_{-\alpha})\neq0$.

So the condition is $\beta=-\alpha$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 4.2.4.** Let $L$ be a semisimple Lie algebra with maximal toral subalgebra $H$ and root space decomposition $L=H\oplus\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Phi}L_\alpha$ ($L_0=H$, $\Phi$ the nonzero roots, $m_\alpha=\dim L_\alpha$). For $\lambda\in H^*$ let $t_\lambda\in H$ be the element with $\kappa(t_\lambda,h)=\lambda(h)$ for all $h\in H$, and $\langle\lambda,\mu\rangle=\kappa(t_\lambda,t_\mu)$. Assume the facts from the text that $\kappa|_H$ is non-degenerate, and that for each root $\alpha$ there is $h_\alpha\in H$ spanning, with elements of $L_{\pm\alpha}$, a copy of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ with $\alpha(h_\alpha)=2$ (so the eigenvalues of $\operatorname{ad}h_\alpha$ are integers, by Problem 3.1.5). Show that $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ is a symmetric bilinear form on $H^*$ that is positive definite on the real span $E$ of the roots.
answer: Symmetric bilinear from $\kappa$; positivity from $\langle\lambda,\lambda\rangle=\sum_\alpha m_\alpha\langle\alpha,\lambda\rangle^2$ with all $\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle$ rational.

solutions.title: Express the form through the roots
solutions.body:
**Bilinear and symmetric.** $\lambda\mapsto t_\lambda$ is linear (by uniqueness in the definition) and $\kappa$ is symmetric bilinear, so $\langle\lambda,\mu\rangle=\kappa(t_\lambda,t_\mu)$ is symmetric bilinear.

**Formula.** Compute $\kappa(h,h')=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{ad}h\operatorname{ad}h')$ in a basis of root vectors: $\operatorname{ad}h$ acts by $0$ on $H$ and by $\alpha(h)$ on $L_\alpha$, so
$$\kappa(h,h')=\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi}m_\alpha\,\alpha(h)\alpha(h').$$
Taking $h=h'=t_\lambda$: $\langle\lambda,\lambda\rangle=\sum_\alpha m_\alpha\,\alpha(t_\lambda)^2=\sum_\alpha m_\alpha\langle\alpha,\lambda\rangle^2$ (as $\alpha(t_\lambda)=\kappa(t_\alpha,t_\lambda)$).

**Rationality.** By Problem 4.2.6, $h_\alpha=2t_\alpha/\langle\alpha,\alpha\rangle$ and $\beta(h_\alpha)\in\mathbb Z$ (eigenvalues of $\operatorname{ad}h_\alpha$ are integers). So $\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle=\tfrac12\langle\alpha,\alpha\rangle\beta(h_\alpha)$. Applying the formula to $\lambda=\alpha$: $\langle\alpha,\alpha\rangle=\sum_\gamma m_\gamma\big(\tfrac12\langle\alpha,\alpha\rangle\gamma(h_\alpha)\big)^2$, so $\langle\alpha,\alpha\rangle=4\big/\sum_\gamma m_\gamma\gamma(h_\alpha)^2$, a positive rational (the sum is a sum of integer squares including $\gamma=\alpha$, value $4m_\alpha$, hence positive). Therefore all $\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle$ are rational.

**Positivity.** Let $\lambda\in E$ be a real combination of roots. Since all $\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle$ are rational, each $\langle\alpha,\lambda\rangle$ is real, so $\langle\lambda,\lambda\rangle=\sum m_\alpha\langle\alpha,\lambda\rangle^2\ge0$, with equality only if $\langle\alpha,\lambda\rangle=\alpha(t_\lambda)=0$ for every root $\alpha$. The roots span $H^*$ (if all roots vanish on $h\in H$ then $\kappa(h,h')=0$ for all $h'\in H$, so $h=0$ since $\kappa|_H$ is non-degenerate), hence $t_\lambda=0$, i.e. $\lambda=0$. Thus $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ is a real inner product on $E$. $\blacksquare$

reviewNote: As printed the claim is that the form is an inner product on the complex space H*; a positive-definite statement only makes sense over the real span of the roots, which is what the proof shows (the official solution is a sketch).

prompt: **Problem 4.2.5.** In the setting of a semisimple Lie algebra $L$ with maximal toral subalgebra $H=L_0$ and root spaces $L_\lambda$, let $t_\lambda\in H$ be defined by $\kappa(t_\lambda,h)=\lambda(h)$ for $h\in H$. Show that $[x,y]=\kappa(x,y)\,t_\lambda$ for $x\in L_\lambda$, $y\in L_{-\lambda}$.
answer: $[x,y]\in H$ and pairing both sides against $h\in H$ gives equal values.

solutions.title: Pair with $H$
solutions.body:
First, $[L_\alpha,L_\beta]\subseteq L_{\alpha+\beta}$: for $h\in H$, $[h,[x,y]]=[[h,x],y]+[x,[h,y]]=(\alpha+\beta)(h)[x,y]$ (derivation property, Problem 3.4.6). So $[x,y]\in L_0=H$.

For any $h\in H$, using invariance of $\kappa$ (Problem 4.1.2),
$$\kappa(h,[x,y])=\kappa([h,x],y)=\lambda(h)\kappa(x,y)=\kappa(t_\lambda,h)\kappa(x,y)=\kappa\big(h,\kappa(x,y)t_\lambda\big).$$
Hence $\kappa\big(h,[x,y]-\kappa(x,y)t_\lambda\big)=0$ for all $h\in H$. The element $[x,y]-\kappa(x,y)t_\lambda$ lies in $H$, and $\kappa|_H$ is non-degenerate (Problem 4.2.3 with $\alpha=0$: $\kappa(L_0,L_\gamma)=0$ for $\gamma\ne0$, so non-degeneracy of $\kappa$ forces non-degeneracy on $L_0=H$). Therefore $[x,y]=\kappa(x,y)t_\lambda$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 4.2.6.** For a root $\lambda$ let $e_\lambda\in L_\lambda$, $f_\lambda\in L_{-\lambda}$, $h_\lambda\in H$ span a copy of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ (with $h_\lambda=[e_\lambda,f_\lambda]$ and $\lambda(h_\lambda)=2$), and $t_\lambda\in H$ satisfies $\kappa(t_\lambda,h)=\lambda(h)$. Show that $h_\lambda=\dfrac{2t_\lambda}{\kappa(t_\lambda,t_\lambda)}$ and $\kappa(t_\lambda,t_\lambda)\kappa(h_\lambda,h_\lambda)=4$.
answer: Apply $[x,y]=\kappa(x,y)t_\lambda$ to $e_\lambda,f_\lambda$ and evaluate $\lambda(h_\lambda)=2$.

solutions.title: Solve for $h_\lambda$
solutions.body:
By Problem 4.2.5, $h_\lambda=[e_\lambda,f_\lambda]=\kappa(e_\lambda,f_\lambda)\,t_\lambda$. Then
$$2=\lambda(h_\lambda)=\kappa(t_\lambda,h_\lambda)=\kappa(e_\lambda,f_\lambda)\,\kappa(t_\lambda,t_\lambda).$$
So $\kappa(t_\lambda,t_\lambda)\neq0$ and $\kappa(e_\lambda,f_\lambda)=2/\kappa(t_\lambda,t_\lambda)$, giving $h_\lambda=\dfrac{2t_\lambda}{\kappa(t_\lambda,t_\lambda)}$. Then
$$\kappa(h_\lambda,h_\lambda)=\frac{4\kappa(t_\lambda,t_\lambda)}{\kappa(t_\lambda,t_\lambda)^2}=\frac{4}{\kappa(t_\lambda,t_\lambda)},$$
so $\kappa(t_\lambda,t_\lambda)\kappa(h_\lambda,h_\lambda)=4$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 5.1.1.** Let $V$ be a real vector space with an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$. A subset $R\subset V$ (not a subspace) is a *root system* of $V$ if $\operatorname{span}R=V$ and for all $v,w\in R$: (1) the only scalar multiples of $v$ in $R$ are $\pm v$; (2) $w-\dfrac{2\langle v,w\rangle}{\langle v,v\rangle}v\in R$; (3) $\dfrac{2\langle v,w\rangle}{\langle v,v\rangle}\in\mathbb Z$. A root system is *reducible* if $R=R_1\cup R_2$ with nonempty $R_1,R_2$, $\langle v_1,v_2\rangle=0$ for $v_i\in R_i$, and each $R_i$ a root system (of its span); otherwise irreducible. A *base* $B\subset R$ is a basis of $V$ such that every $w\in R$ is $\pm\sum_{v\in B}c(v)v$ with integers $c(v)\ge0$. Find all root systems in $\mathbb R$.
answer: $R=\{r,-r\}$ for any real $r\neq0$.

solutions.title: Check the axioms
solutions.body: $R$ must span $\mathbb R$, so it contains some $r\ne0$; by (1) every root is $\pm r$, and $-r\in R$ by (2) with $v=w=r$ ($r-2r=-r$). Hence $R=\{r,-r\}$. Conversely $\{r,-r\}$ satisfies (1), (2) (reflection sends $\pm r\mapsto\mp r$) and (3) ($2\langle v,w\rangle/\langle v,v\rangle=\pm2$). $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 5.1.2.** Let $V$ be a real vector space with an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$. A subset $R\subset V$ (not a subspace) is a *root system* of $V$ if $\operatorname{span}R=V$ and for all $v,w\in R$: (1) the only scalar multiples of $v$ in $R$ are $\pm v$; (2) $w-\dfrac{2\langle v,w\rangle}{\langle v,v\rangle}v\in R$; (3) $\dfrac{2\langle v,w\rangle}{\langle v,v\rangle}\in\mathbb Z$. A root system is *reducible* if $R=R_1\cup R_2$ with nonempty $R_1,R_2$, $\langle v_1,v_2\rangle=0$ for $v_i\in R_i$, and each $R_i$ a root system (of its span); otherwise irreducible. A *base* $B\subset R$ is a basis of $V$ such that every $w\in R$ is $\pm\sum_{v\in B}c(v)v$ with integers $c(v)\ge0$. For $v\neq\pm w$ in a root system, let $\varphi$ be the angle between them ($\langle v,w\rangle=\|v\|\|w\|\cos\varphi$). Using that $v,w$ may be interchanged in condition (3), show that $4\cos^2\varphi\in\{0,1,2,3\}$.
answer: $4\cos^2\varphi$ is a product of two integers, nonnegative, and $<4$.

solutions.title: Product of two integers
solutions.body:
By (3), $a=\dfrac{2\langle v,w\rangle}{\langle v,v\rangle}$ and $b=\dfrac{2\langle v,w\rangle}{\langle w,w\rangle}$ are integers, and
$$ab=\frac{4\langle v,w\rangle^2}{\|v\|^2\|w\|^2}=4\cos^2\varphi .$$
So $4\cos^2\varphi$ is an integer in $[0,4]$. It equals $4$ iff $\cos\varphi=\pm1$ iff $w$ is a multiple of $v$, i.e. $w=\pm v$ by (1), excluded. So $4\cos^2\varphi\in\{0,1,2,3\}$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 5.1.3.** Let $V$ be a real vector space with an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$. A subset $R\subset V$ (not a subspace) is a *root system* of $V$ if $\operatorname{span}R=V$ and for all $v,w\in R$: (1) the only scalar multiples of $v$ in $R$ are $\pm v$; (2) $w-\dfrac{2\langle v,w\rangle}{\langle v,v\rangle}v\in R$; (3) $\dfrac{2\langle v,w\rangle}{\langle v,v\rangle}\in\mathbb Z$. A root system is *reducible* if $R=R_1\cup R_2$ with nonempty $R_1,R_2$, $\langle v_1,v_2\rangle=0$ for $v_i\in R_i$, and each $R_i$ a root system (of its span); otherwise irreducible. A *base* $B\subset R$ is a basis of $V$ such that every $w\in R$ is $\pm\sum_{v\in B}c(v)v$ with integers $c(v)\ge0$. Using the standard dot product, find all root systems of $\mathbb R^2$ up to rotation, dilation and (independent) rescaling of orthogonal components.
answer: Four: $A_1\times A_1$ (e.g. $\pm(2,0),\pm(0,1)$), $A_2$ (6 roots, equal length, $60^\circ$ apart), $B_2$ (8 roots, lengths $1,\sqrt2$, $45^\circ$ apart), $G_2$ (12 roots, lengths $1,\sqrt3$, $30^\circ$ apart).

solutions.title: Classify by the smallest angle
solutions.body:
**Possible angles.** By Problem 5.1.2 the angle between two non-proportional roots is in $\{90^\circ,60^\circ,120^\circ,45^\circ,135^\circ,30^\circ,150^\circ\}$.

**Structure.** Let $\theta>0$ be the smallest angle between two distinct roots, and $\alpha,\beta$ roots at angle $\theta$ (so $\theta\le90^\circ$ since $-\beta$ is also a root). Reflection in the line perpendicular to a root $v$ (condition (2)) maps $R$ to itself, and the product of the reflections for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ is the rotation by $2\theta$. So $R$ is invariant under rotation by $2\theta$; starting from $\alpha$ and $\beta=\alpha$ rotated by $\theta$, the rotations by multiples of $2\theta$ produce roots in all directions $\alpha+j\theta$, $j\in\mathbb Z$. Any other root $\gamma$ lies between consecutive such directions at an angle $<\theta$ from one of them, contradicting the choice of $\theta$ unless it lies on one. So the root directions are exactly the multiples of $\theta$, which forces $\theta\in\{90^\circ,60^\circ,45^\circ,30^\circ\}$ (a divisor of $360^\circ$ in the allowed list).

**Lengths.** For adjacent roots with $4\cos^2\theta=ab$ ($a,b$ the integers of 5.1.2):

- $\theta=90^\circ$: any lengths; the system splits into two orthogonal pairs $\pm u,\pm w$: $A_1\times A_1$ (4 roots).
- $\theta=60^\circ$: $ab=1$, $a=b=1$, equal lengths; all 6 roots have equal length: $A_2$.
- $\theta=45^\circ$: $ab=2$, so $\{a,b\}=\{1,2\}$ and the squared length ratio is $2$; adjacent roots alternate between lengths $\ell$ and $\sqrt2\ell$: $B_2$ (8 roots).
- $\theta=30^\circ$: $ab=3$, squared ratio $3$; roots alternate between $\ell$ and $\sqrt3\ell$: $G_2$ (12 roots).

**They are root systems.** Check that each set is closed under reflections in its roots (dihedral symmetry of the regular $2m$-gon directions with the alternating lengths) and that $2\langle v,w\rangle/\langle v,v\rangle=\pm1,\pm2,\pm3,0$ is an integer. For example $A_2=\{\pm(1,0),\pm(\tfrac12,\tfrac{\sqrt3}2),\pm(-\tfrac12,\tfrac{\sqrt3}2)\}$, $B_2=\{\pm(1,0),\pm(0,1),\pm(1,1),\pm(1,-1)\}$ (all 8 vectors $(\pm1,0),(0,\pm1),(\pm1,\pm1)$), and $G_2$ the 6 short roots $\pm(1,0)$ and rotations by $60^\circ$ plus the 6 long roots of length $\sqrt3$ at angles $30^\circ+60^\circ k$. $\blacksquare$

reviewNote: The paper's ''up to rotation and dilation'' equivalence is ambiguous for A1xA1 (arbitrary relative lengths); I count it as one system, giving the same four systems as the official solution.

prompt: **Problem 5.1.4.** Let $V$ be a real vector space with an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$. A subset $R\subset V$ (not a subspace) is a *root system* of $V$ if $\operatorname{span}R=V$ and for all $v,w\in R$: (1) the only scalar multiples of $v$ in $R$ are $\pm v$; (2) $w-\dfrac{2\langle v,w\rangle}{\langle v,v\rangle}v\in R$; (3) $\dfrac{2\langle v,w\rangle}{\langle v,v\rangle}\in\mathbb Z$. A root system is *reducible* if $R=R_1\cup R_2$ with nonempty $R_1,R_2$, $\langle v_1,v_2\rangle=0$ for $v_i\in R_i$, and each $R_i$ a root system (of its span); otherwise irreducible. A *base* $B\subset R$ is a basis of $V$ such that every $w\in R$ is $\pm\sum_{v\in B}c(v)v$ with integers $c(v)\ge0$. Show that any root system can be written as a union of irreducible root systems (of mutually orthogonal subspaces).
answer: Group roots by the equivalence relation generated by non-orthogonality.

solutions.title: Connected components
solutions.body:
**Classes.** For $v,w\in R$ write $v\sim w$ if there is a chain $v=u_0,u_1,\dots,u_k=w$ in $R$ with $\langle u_{i-1},u_i\rangle\neq0$. This is an equivalence relation with classes $R_1,\dots,R_m$, and roots in different classes are orthogonal. The spans $V_i=\operatorname{span}R_i$ are mutually orthogonal and nonzero, so $m\le\dim V$ and $V=\bigoplus V_i$.

**Each $R_i$ is a root system of $V_i$.** (1) and (3) are inherited. (2): let $v,w\in R_i$ and $c=2\langle v,w\rangle/\langle v,v\rangle$. If $c=0$, then $s_v(w)=w\in R_i$. If $c\ne0$, then $s_v(w)=w-cv\in R$ and $\langle s_v(w),v\rangle=-\langle w,v\rangle\ne0$, so $s_v(w)\sim v\sim w$, i.e. $s_v(w)\in R_i$.

**Irreducibility.** If $R_i=A\cup B$ with $A,B$ nonempty and mutually orthogonal, then no chain joins an element of $A$ to one of $B$, contradicting that $R_i$ is a single class. So each $R_i$ is irreducible and $R=\bigcup R_i$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 5.1.5.** Let $V$ be a real vector space with an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$. A subset $R\subset V$ (not a subspace) is a *root system* of $V$ if $\operatorname{span}R=V$ and for all $v,w\in R$: (1) the only scalar multiples of $v$ in $R$ are $\pm v$; (2) $w-\dfrac{2\langle v,w\rangle}{\langle v,v\rangle}v\in R$; (3) $\dfrac{2\langle v,w\rangle}{\langle v,v\rangle}\in\mathbb Z$. A root system is *reducible* if $R=R_1\cup R_2$ with nonempty $R_1,R_2$, $\langle v_1,v_2\rangle=0$ for $v_i\in R_i$, and each $R_i$ a root system (of its span); otherwise irreducible. A *base* $B\subset R$ is a basis of $V$ such that every $w\in R$ is $\pm\sum_{v\in B}c(v)v$ with integers $c(v)\ge0$. Show that any root system has a base.
answer: Pick $x$ not orthogonal to any root, let $B$ be the indecomposable roots among $R^+=\{v:\langle x,v\rangle>0\}$; show $B$ spans, is independent, and generates $R$.

solutions.title: Indecomposable positive roots
solutions.body:
**Finiteness.** $R$ is finite. Fix a basis $b_1,\dots,b_d\subseteq R$ (possible since $R$ spans). Any $v\in R$ is non-orthogonal to some $b_i$ (the $b_i$ span $V$). If $v\ne\pm b_i$, then with $a=2\langle v,b_i\rangle/\langle v,v\rangle$ and $b=2\langle v,b_i\rangle/\langle b_i,b_i\rangle$ nonzero integers, $ab\in\{1,2,3\}$ (Problem 5.1.2), so $\langle v,v\rangle/\langle b_i,b_i\rangle=b/a\in\{1,2,3,\tfrac12,\tfrac13\}$. Thus all roots have squared length at most $3\max_i\langle b_i,b_i\rangle$. The integers $2\langle v,b_i\rangle/\langle b_i,b_i\rangle$ are then bounded by $2\|v\|/\|b_i\|$, so only finitely many integer vectors occur, and they determine $v$ (the $b_i$ form a basis). So $R$ is finite. Hence the hyperplanes $v^\perp$ ($v\in R$) do not cover $V$, and we can choose $x\in V$ with $\langle x,v\rangle\neq0$ for all $v\in R$. Let $R^+=\{v\in R:\langle x,v\rangle>0\}$; then $R=R^+\sqcup(-R^+)$ (using that $-v\in R$ by (2)). Let $B$ be the set of $v\in R^+$ that are **not** a sum of two elements of $R^+$.

**(a) Every $v\in R^+$ is a nonnegative integer combination of $B$.** Induct on $\langle x,v\rangle$ (finitely many values). If $v\in B$ done; otherwise $v=v_1+v_2$ with $v_i\in R^+$ and $\langle x,v_i\rangle<\langle x,v\rangle$, so induction applies to $v_1,v_2$.

**(b) $\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle\le0$ for distinct $\alpha,\beta\in B$.** Suppose $\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle>0$. Then $a=2\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle/\langle\beta,\beta\rangle$ and $b=2\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle/\langle\alpha,\alpha\rangle$ are positive integers with $ab\le3$ (as $\alpha\ne\pm\beta$), so $a=1$ or $b=1$. By (2), $\alpha-a\beta\in R$ and $\beta-b\alpha\in R$; hence $\alpha-\beta\in R$ (if $a=1$) or $\beta-\alpha\in R$ (if $b=1$), and since $R=-R$ both are roots. One of them lies in $R^+$. If $\alpha-\beta\in R^+$ then $\alpha=(\alpha-\beta)+\beta$ is decomposable; if $\beta-\alpha\in R^+$ then $\beta=(\beta-\alpha)+\alpha$ is decomposable. Contradiction.

**(c) $B$ is linearly independent.** Suppose a nontrivial relation exists; separate positive and negative coefficients: $y=\sum_{i\in P}p_i\alpha_i=\sum_{j\in N}n_j\beta_j$ with $p_i,n_j>0$ and $P\cap N=\emptyset$. Then $\langle y,y\rangle=\sum p_in_j\langle\alpha_i,\beta_j\rangle\le0$ by (b), so $y=0$. But $0=\langle x,y\rangle=\sum p_i\langle x,\alpha_i\rangle>0$ unless $P=\emptyset$; similarly $N=\emptyset$. So the relation is trivial.

**(d) $B$ is a base.** By (a), $R^+$, hence $R=R^+\cup-R^+$, is contained in the $\mathbb Z$-span of $B$ with every root having all coefficients of one sign. Since $R$ spans $V$, so does $B$; with (c), $B$ is a basis of $V$, and every root is $\pm\sum c(v)v$ with $c(v)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 5.2.2.** Let $B$ be a base of a root system and normalize it to unit vectors $B'$; then $\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\le0$ for $i\ne j$ and $4\langle v_i,v_j\rangle^2\in\{0,1,2,3\}$. The *Dynkin diagram* has a node for each element of $B'$ and $e(v,w)=4\langle v,w\rangle^2$ edges between $v$ and $w$ (an arrow pointing to the shorter root of the original base when $e\ge2$). Show that no Dynkin diagram may have a cycle.
answer: For unit vectors $v_1,\dots,v_n$ with $\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\le0$ and $2|\langle v_i,v_j\rangle|\ge1$ on edges, $\|\sum v_i\|^2>0$ forces fewer edges than vertices.

solutions.title: Count edges
solutions.body:
Let $v_1,\dots,v_n$ be the (unit) vectors of any subset of nodes; they are independent (part of a basis), so $v=\sum v_i\neq0$ and
$$0<\langle v,v\rangle=n+2\sum_{i<j}\langle v_i,v_j\rangle .$$
For connected $v_i,v_j$ we have $4\langle v_i,v_j\rangle^2\in\{1,2,3\}$ and $\langle v_i,v_j\rangle<0$, so $-2\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\ge1$; non-connected pairs contribute $0$. Hence $n>\sum_{i<j}(-2\langle v_i,v_j\rangle)\ge C$, where $C$ is the number of connected pairs. So any set of $n$ nodes spans fewer than $n$ connected pairs.

A cycle of length $k$ would be $k$ nodes with at least $k$ connected pairs, a contradiction. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 5.2.3.** Let $B$ be a base of a root system and normalize it to unit vectors $B'$; then $\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\le0$ for $i\ne j$ and $4\langle v_i,v_j\rangle^2\in\{0,1,2,3\}$. The *Dynkin diagram* has a node for each element of $B'$ and $e(v,w)=4\langle v,w\rangle^2$ edges between $v$ and $w$ (an arrow pointing to the shorter root of the original base when $e\ge2$). Show that no node in a Dynkin diagram has more than three total edges attached to it (counting a double edge as $2$, a triple edge as $3$).
answer: Project the unit vector $v$ onto the span of its (mutually orthogonal) neighbours: $\sum\langle v,v_i\rangle^2<1$.

solutions.title: Bessel's inequality
solutions.body:
Let $v$ be a node with neighbours $v_1,\dots,v_k$ (unit vectors). There are no cycles (5.2.2), so the neighbours are pairwise non-adjacent, i.e. pairwise orthogonal. Since $v$ is not in the span of $v_1,\dots,v_k$ (base elements are independent),
$$1=\langle v,v\rangle>\sum_{i=1}^k\langle v,v_i\rangle^2 .$$
(The right side is the squared length of the orthogonal projection of $v$ onto $\operatorname{span}\{v_i\}$.) Multiplying by $4$: $\sum_i e(v,v_i)<4$, so the total number of edges at $v$ is at most $3$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 5.2.4.** Let $B$ be a base of a root system and normalize it to unit vectors $B'$; then $\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\le0$ for $i\ne j$ and $4\langle v_i,v_j\rangle^2\in\{0,1,2,3\}$. The *Dynkin diagram* has a node for each element of $B'$ and $e(v,w)=4\langle v,w\rangle^2$ edges between $v$ and $w$ (an arrow pointing to the shorter root of the original base when $e\ge2$). Assume the **Shrinking Lemma**: if a Dynkin diagram has nodes $v_1,\dots,v_n$ forming a line of single edges, then replacing them by the single node $v=\sum v_i$ (attached to whatever the ends were attached to) gives the Dynkin diagram of a base of a root system. Use it, together with Problems 5.2.2 and 5.2.3, to show that a connected Dynkin diagram cannot have more than one branch node (node with three neighbours), more than one double edge, or both a branch node and a double edge.
answer: Shrink the single-edge path between two such features into one node, which would then have $4$ edges.

solutions.title: Contract the path
solutions.body:
The diagram is a tree (5.2.2). Suppose it has two "features", each a branch node (three single edges) or a double edge. Choose two features with no feature strictly between them and let $P$ be the path joining them. All edges of $P$ are single (a double edge on $P$ would be a feature between or at an end, and we take the ends to be the nodes $A$ and $B$ of the features closest to each other, so the path between $A$ and $B$ has only single edges and interior nodes of degree $2$).

Shrink the line $P$ (from $A$ to $B$ inclusive) to one node $v=\sum_{u\in P}u$. By the Shrinking Lemma this is still a valid Dynkin diagram, and the edges at $v$ are those leaving $P$ at $A$ and at $B$: the two remaining single edges at $A$ if $A$ is a branch node (the third edge lies on $P$), or the double edge at $A$ if $A$ is the end of a double edge; similarly at $B$.

- Two branch nodes: $v$ has $2+2=4$ single edges.
- Two double edges: $v$ has $2+2=4$ edges.
- Branch node and double edge: $v$ has $2+2=4$ edges.

Each violates Problem 5.2.3 (at most $3$ edges). Hence there is at most one feature in total: at most one branch node or one double edge, and not both. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 5.2.5.** Let $B$ be a base of a root system and normalize it to unit vectors $B'$; then $\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\le0$ for $i\ne j$ and $4\langle v_i,v_j\rangle^2\in\{0,1,2,3\}$. The *Dynkin diagram* has a node for each element of $B'$ and $e(v,w)=4\langle v,w\rangle^2$ edges between $v$ and $w$ (an arrow pointing to the shorter root of the original base when $e\ge2$). Prove that if a connected Dynkin diagram has a double edge whose two ends are both attached to further nodes, then the diagram is $F_4$ (four nodes in a line with a double edge in the middle).
answer: By 5.2.4 the diagram is a path $v_1\cdots v_m=w_n\cdots w_1$; Cauchy-Schwarz on the combined vectors gives $(m-1)(n-1)<2$.

solutions.title: Cauchy-Schwarz on the two sides
solutions.body:
By Problem 5.2.4 a diagram with a double edge has no branch node, so (being connected, a tree with all degrees $\le2$) it is a path: $v_1,\dots,v_m$ joined by single edges, a double edge between $v_m$ and $w_n$, then $w_n,\dots,w_1$ with single edges; "both ends attached to other nodes" means $m,n\ge2$.

Let $v=\sum_{i=1}^m iv_i$ and $w=\sum_{j=1}^n jw_j$ (so $v_m$ and $w_n$ carry the largest coefficients $m$, $n$). As in the model proof (a line of $k$ unit vectors joined by single edges and $\langle v_i,v_{i+1}\rangle=-\tfrac12$), $\langle v,v\rangle=\frac{m(m+1)}2$ and $\langle w,w\rangle=\frac{n(n+1)}2$. Only $v_m,w_n$ are connected between the two sides, with $\langle v_m,w_n\rangle^2=\tfrac12$, so
$$\langle v,w\rangle^2=m^2n^2\langle v_m,w_n\rangle^2=\frac{m^2n^2}2.$$
$v,w$ are not parallel (they involve disjoint independent sets), so Cauchy-Schwarz is strict:
$$\frac{m^2n^2}2<\frac{m(m+1)}2\cdot\frac{n(n+1)}2\iff 2mn<(m+1)(n+1)\iff(m-1)(n-1)<2.$$
With $m,n\ge2$ this forces $m=n=2$: four nodes in a line with the middle edge double, i.e. $F_4$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 5.2.6.** Let $B$ be a base of a root system and normalize it to unit vectors $B'$; then $\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\le0$ for $i\ne j$ and $4\langle v_i,v_j\rangle^2\in\{0,1,2,3\}$. The *Dynkin diagram* has a node for each element of $B'$ and $e(v,w)=4\langle v,w\rangle^2$ edges between $v$ and $w$ (an arrow pointing to the shorter root of the original base when $e\ge2$). Consider a connected Dynkin diagram with a branch node $z$ (three neighbours). Show that one of the three arms from $z$ has length $1$ (a single node), and that for the other two arms: if one has length $1$ the third may have any length; if one has length $2$, the third has length at most $4$. (Arm lengths count nodes, not including $z$; all edges are single by Problem 5.2.4.)
answer: With arm lengths $n\ge m\ge p$: $\frac1{n+1}+\frac1{m+1}+\frac1{p+1}>1$, giving $p=1$, and $m=1$ ($n$ arbitrary) or $m=2$, $n\le4$.

solutions.title: Project $z$ onto the arms
solutions.body:
All edges are single (5.2.4 forbids a double edge together with a branch node), so each arm is a line with $\langle u_i,u_{i+1}\rangle=-\tfrac12$. Let the arms have $n,m,p$ nodes; label the nodes of an arm $x_1,\dots,x_n$ with $x_n$ adjacent to $z$, and put $x=\sum_{i=1}^nix_i$; define $w$ and $v$ likewise for the other arms. By the line computation of the text, $\langle x,x\rangle=\frac{n(n+1)}2$, and $\langle z,x\rangle=n\langle z,x_n\rangle=-\frac n2$. The vectors $x,w,v$ are pairwise orthogonal (the arms are disjoint and, in a tree, not connected to each other except through $z$). Let $x'=x/\|x\|$, etc.; then
$$\langle z,x'\rangle^2=\frac{n^2/4}{n(n+1)/2}=\frac{n}{2(n+1)}.$$
Since $z$ is a unit vector not in the span of $x',w',v'$,
$$1>\frac n{2(n+1)}+\frac m{2(m+1)}+\frac p{2(p+1)}\iff\frac1{n+1}+\frac1{m+1}+\frac1{p+1}>1.$$
Assume $n\ge m\ge p\ge1$. Then $\frac3{p+1}>1$, so $p<2$, $p=1$. Then $\frac1{n+1}+\frac1{m+1}>\frac12$, and $\frac2{m+1}>\frac12$ gives $m<3$: $m\in\{1,2\}$. If $m=1$ the condition holds for every $n$. If $m=2$: $\frac1{n+1}>\frac12-\frac13=\frac16$, so $n\le4$. So one arm has length $1$; of the other two, if one has length $1$ the third is arbitrary, and if one has length $2$ the other has length at most $4$. $\blacksquare$

solutions.title: Roots, base, inner products
solutions.body:
Index rows/columns $0,1,\dots,2n$ (row $0$ is the extra one). By Problem 2.2.2 the algebra consists of $\begin{pmatrix}0&-(R_{2n}w)^T\\w&Y\end{pmatrix}$ with $Y\in\mathfrak{so}_{2n}$. Let $\mathfrak h=\{h=\sum_{i=1}^nc_i(E_{i,i}-E_{i+n,i+n})\}$ (diagonal, in the algebra). The following elements lie in the algebra and are $\operatorname{ad}\mathfrak h$-eigenvectors:

- $m_{i,j}=E_{i,j}-E_{j+n,i+n}$ ($i\ne j$): eigenvalue $c_i-c_j$, root $\lambda_i-\lambda_j$.
- $p_{i,j}=E_{i,j+n}-E_{j,i+n}$ ($i<j$): $c_i+c_j$, root $\lambda_i+\lambda_j$; and their transposes $p_{i,j}^T$: root $-\lambda_i-\lambda_j$.
- $B_i=E_{i,0}-E_{0,i+n}$: eigenvalue $c_i$, root $\lambda_i$; $C_i=E_{0,i}-E_{i+n,0}$: root $-\lambda_i$.

The numbers: $n+n(n-1)+n(n-1)+2n=2n^2+n=\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}$, so these are all root vectors and the roots are $\pm\lambda_i\pm\lambda_j$ ($i<j$) and $\pm\lambda_i$.

**Base.** Take $\alpha_i=\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}$ ($1\le i\le n-1$) and $\beta=\lambda_n$. They form a basis of $\mathfrak h^*$ ($n$ elements, triangular in the $\lambda$'s), and every root is $\pm$ a nonnegative combination: $\lambda_i-\lambda_j=\sum_{k=i}^{j-1}\alpha_k$; $\lambda_i=\sum_{k=i}^{n-1}\alpha_k+\beta$; $\lambda_i+\lambda_j=\sum_{k=i}^{n-1}\alpha_k+\sum_{k=j}^{n-1}\alpha_k+2\beta$.

**Inner products** (take $\langle\lambda_i,\lambda_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}$ after scaling): $\langle\alpha_i,\alpha_i\rangle=2$, $\langle\alpha_i,\alpha_{i+1}\rangle=-1$, $\langle\alpha_i,\alpha_j\rangle=0$ for $|i-j|>1$, $\langle\beta,\beta\rangle=1$, $\langle\alpha_{n-1},\beta\rangle=-1$, $\langle\alpha_i,\beta\rangle=0$ for $i<n-1$.

**Edges.** $e(\alpha_i,\alpha_{i+1})=4\cdot1/(2\cdot2)=1$; $e(\alpha_{n-1},\beta)=4\cdot1/(2\cdot1)=2$. So the diagram is a line $\alpha_1-\alpha_2-\cdots-\alpha_{n-1}\Rightarrow\beta$ with a double edge at the end, the arrow pointing to the shorter root $\beta$ (since $\|\beta\|^2=1<2=\|\alpha_{n-1}\|^2$). This is type $B_n$ ($n=1$: a single node). $\blacksquare$

$\mathfrak h=\{\operatorname{diag}(c_1,\dots,c_n):\sum c_i=0\}$, $\dim n-1$. For $i\ne j$, $[h,E_{i,j}]=(c_i-c_j)E_{i,j}$, so the roots are $\lambda_i-\lambda_j$ with root vectors $E_{i,j}$. These $n(n-1)$ vectors together with $\mathfrak h$ give all $n^2-1$ dimensions.

answer: $C_n$: nodes $\alpha_i=\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}$ ($1\le i<n$) and $\beta=2\lambda_n$ in a line, with a double edge between $\alpha_{n-1}$ and $\beta$ pointing from the longer root $\beta$ to $\alpha_{n-1}$ (for $n=1$ a single node).

solutions.title: Roots, base, inner products
solutions.body:
By Problem 2.2.2, $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}=\Big\{\begin{pmatrix}M&P\\Q&-M^T\end{pmatrix}:P,Q\text{ symmetric}\Big\}$. Take $\mathfrak h=\{\sum c_i(E_{i,i}-E_{i+n,i+n})\}$. Eigenvectors:

- $m_{i,j}=E_{i,j}-E_{j+n,i+n}$ ($i\neq j$): root $\lambda_i-\lambda_j$.
- $p_{i,j}=E_{i,j+n}+E_{j,i+n}$ ($i<j$): root $\lambda_i+\lambda_j$; $p_{i,i}=E_{i,i+n}$: root $2\lambda_i$; their transposes: roots $-\lambda_i-\lambda_j$ and $-2\lambda_i$.

Count: $n+n(n-1)+2\cdot\frac{n(n-1)}2+2n=2n^2+n$, so these are all the roots: $\pm\lambda_i\pm\lambda_j$ ($i<j$), $\pm2\lambda_i$.

**Base.** $\alpha_i=\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}$ ($i<n$) and $\beta=2\lambda_n$. Every root is a nonnegative combination: $\lambda_i-\lambda_j=\sum_{k=i}^{j-1}\alpha_k$; $\lambda_i+\lambda_j=\sum_{k=i}^{n-1}\alpha_k+\sum_{k=j}^{n-1}\alpha_k+\beta$ (for $j=n$ the second sum is empty); $2\lambda_i=2\sum_{k=i}^{n-1}\alpha_k+\beta$.

**Inner products** (with $\langle\lambda_i,\lambda_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}$ after scaling): $\langle\alpha_i,\alpha_i\rangle=2$, $\langle\alpha_i,\alpha_{i+1}\rangle=-1$, $\langle\beta,\beta\rangle=4$, $\langle\alpha_{n-1},\beta\rangle=-2$, others $0$.

**Edges.** $e(\alpha_i,\alpha_{i+1})=1$ and $e(\alpha_{n-1},\beta)=4\cdot4/(2\cdot4)=2$. So the diagram is a line $\alpha_1-\cdots-\alpha_{n-1}\Leftarrow\beta$ with a double edge at the end, the arrow pointing from the longer root $\beta$ ($\|\beta\|^2=4$) to $\alpha_{n-1}$ ($\|\alpha_{n-1}\|^2=2$). This is type $C_n$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 5.3.2.** Using Serre's theorem (two Lie algebras with the same Dynkin diagram are isomorphic) and the Dynkin diagrams of the classical Lie algebras $\mathfrak{sl}_n$ ($A_{n-1}$), $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}$ ($B_n$), $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}$ ($C_n$), $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}$ ($D_n$), state all isomorphisms between them and the diagrams that give them. Do not construct the isomorphisms.
answer: $\mathfrak{so}_3\cong\mathfrak{sp}_2\cong\mathfrak{sl}_2$ (type $A_1=B_1=C_1$); $\mathfrak{so}_5\cong\mathfrak{sp}_4$ ($B_2=C_2$); $\mathfrak{so}_6\cong\mathfrak{sl}_4$ ($D_3=A_3$); also $\mathfrak{so}_4\cong\mathfrak{sl}_2\oplus\mathfrak{sl}_2$ ($D_2=A_1\times A_1$).

solutions.title: Compare diagrams
solutions.body:
The diagrams are:

- $\mathfrak{sl}_{n+1}$: $A_n$ (line of $n$ single-edge nodes), $n\ge1$.
- $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}$: $B_n$ (line of $n$ nodes, last edge double, arrow to the short end), $n\ge1$.
- $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}$: $C_n$ (as $B_n$ with the arrow reversed), $n\ge1$.
- $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}$: $D_n$ (line of $n-2$ nodes with two nodes attached to the last), $n\ge2$ (for $n=2$ two isolated nodes, for $n=3$ a line of three nodes).

Two diagrams in these families coincide only for small $n$:

- $n=1$: $A_1,B_1,C_1$ are all a single node: $\mathfrak{sl}_2\cong\mathfrak{so}_3\cong\mathfrak{sp}_2$.
- $B_2$ and $C_2$ are two nodes with a double edge (the arrow direction only flips the labelling of nodes): $\mathfrak{so}_5\cong\mathfrak{sp}_4$.
- $D_3$ is a line of three single-edge nodes, which is $A_3$: $\mathfrak{so}_6\cong\mathfrak{sl}_4$.
- $D_2$ is two disconnected nodes, i.e. $A_1\times A_1$: $\mathfrak{so}_4\cong\mathfrak{sl}_2\oplus\mathfrak{sl}_2$ (not simple).

For all other $n$ the diagrams are pairwise different: $A_n$ has no double edge and no branch; $B_n,C_n$ ($n\ge3$) have a double edge with different arrow directions; $D_n$ ($n\ge4$) has a branch node. Isomorphic Lie algebras have the same Dynkin diagram, so there are no other isomorphisms; Serre's theorem gives the isomorphisms listed above. $\blacksquare$
